⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “It just works” is one of the phrases most commonly associated with Apple.
  • Of course, it’s now commonly used ironically when Apple products don’t do what they are supposed to (Apple Home, I’m looking at you), but I do think that it’s absolutely the right philosophy and goal – most of the time ….
  • Macworld referenced an Apple brochure from 1996 entitled “Why do people prefer Macintosh?” This is a collection of testimonials from customers, a number of whom use the “it just works” phrasing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“It just works” is one of the phrases most commonly associated with Apple. Interestingly, it appears to have been coined by the manufacturer’s customers and then used by reviewers before it was later picked up by Steve Jobs.

Of course, it’s now commonly used ironically when Apple products don’t do what they are supposed to (Apple Home, I’m looking at you), but I do think that it’s absolutely the right philosophy and goal – most of the time ….

Macworld referenced an Apple brochure from 1996 entitled “Why do people prefer Macintosh?” This is a collection of testimonials from customers, a number of whom use the “it just works” phrasing. It was subsequently used by a number of reviewers. The earliest example I can find of Steve Jobs adopting it was in 1999, when discussing the rollout of FireWire to the Mac in the PowerMac G3.

Industry observers note that it’s hot-pluggable. You don’t have to turn your computer off to connect and disconnect peripherals, you can just plug them right in. Again, the drivers are dynamically loaded. There are no terminators and there are no switches. It just works.

(If you have a link to any earlier example, please do let me know in the comments.).

I’m a major fan of the philosophy. Most of the time, customers should just be able to get on with the tasks they want to execute without having to worry about the technology. The tech that makes it all possible should sit there quietly in the background.

However, there are cases where I think Apple takes this approach a little too far, and where tech-savvy users at least would like a little more transparency and control.

In a recent development, airPods firmware updates are a good example. Back in September, there was quite a significant update in the form of custom EQ. It’s a rather basic version, but still a feature many had wanted for a long time. Instead of being able to manually trigger the update, users had to wait until it “just worked.”.

Apple’s support document has a how-to guide that is essentially an outline of the conditions required to permit an upgrade, and an instruction to simply wait until it happens. Which you will only know by repeatedly checking.

In a recent development, make sure your AirPods are connected via Bluetooth to your iPhone, iPad or Mac. Connect your charging case to a power source. Put your AirPods in their charging case and close the lid. Keep the lid of the charging case closed, and keep your AirPods in Bluetooth range of your iPhone, iPad or Mac. Wait at least 30 minutes for the firmware to be updated. Check the firmware version again.

Recent findings suggest that another example, and one I’ve complained about before, is that there is no way to manually trigger an iCloud document sync, nor any progress indicator when it does finally happen. In the best of cases, it takes seconds; in the worst, many hours. And again, the only way to find out is to repeatedly check.

It’s the same story when shooting a video on your iPhone. Will it still be there an hour later, available to instantly edit and view? Maybe, or maybe it will have been offloaded to the cloud, requiring it to be downloaded before you can do anything with it – while a video you shot months earlier is still stored locally on the device! You can, of course, switch off optimization altogether, but if you choose to use it, you get no control over it. I want a setting that allows me to do things like specify local retention of all photos and videos taken within the past fortnight.

Recent findings suggest that will that video be available in the Mac Photos app when you check half an hour later? Maybe, maybe not. You can click the Sync Now button as many times as you like, and it will apparently have no effect, claiming it’s up to date despite the video being entirely absent. It will be there when it’s there.

Once it is in the Photos app on your Mac, it’s a similar story when exporting it to a folder. You can drag and drop the video into the folder, and this time you are manually triggering the transfer (yay!), but there will be absolutely no visual indication that it is in progress. No grayed-out icon, no progress bar, nothing. So far as the user interface is concerned, it appears that your drag and drop had no effect – until the video file finally appears.

I think with all of these things and more, Apple needs to offer options. Yes, most non-tech customers may be perfectly happy to just wait until things happen, but there ought to be a standard way to trigger things that currently happen in their own sweet time, as well as progress indicators and confirmation that a process is complete.

Is this an ecosystem-wide improvement you’d like to see? Please share your thoughts in the comments and add any frustrating examples of your own.

#109227. 10 Most Universally Loved Power Rangers Seasons, Ranked

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2298 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Screenrant ↗ Open Full Page

10 Most Universally Loved Power Rangers Seasons, Ranked

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2298 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Screenrant

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Power Rangers has always been defined by reinvention.
  • Recent findings suggest that still, even among the best Power Rangers highlights, there’s only a handful whose quality seems beyond debating.
  • Saving civilians feels like the central purpose of Power Rangers Lightspeed Rescue, and that clarity gives the season enormous appeal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Power Rangers has always been defined by reinvention. Across more than 30 years, the franchise has introduced dozens of Ranger teams, regularly swapping familiar faces, powers, and villains while still staying true to its ever-endearing central concept. However, every new incarnation was a risk. Some became instant favorites, while others leave fans counting the episodes until the next team arrives. Fortunately, Power Rangers has produced considerably more hits than misses, with its strongest demonstrates demonstrating just how much variety the core idea of a team of Zord-piloting heroes in colorful suits can accommodate.

Recent findings suggest that still, even among the best Power Rangers highlights, there’s only a handful whose quality seems beyond debating. These are the seasons that regularly unite fans who otherwise disagree about almost everything. They’re the Power Rangers series that manage to capture everything there is to love about the franchise with almost no criticisms from anywhere within the fandom. They represent a wide variety of eras and central gimmicks, but all of them manage to tap into the essence of what makes Power Rangers fans fall in love with the Rangers and their three-decade-plus battle against evil.

Saving civilians feels like the central purpose of Power Rangers Lightspeed Rescue, and that clarity gives the season enormous appeal. Airing in 2000 during the original Saban era, it follows adults recruited to defend Mariner Bay from demons using powers developed through human technology. Firefighter Carter Grayson (Sean Cw Johnson) embodies the appeal. Helping people was already his purpose long before a Morpher entered the picture and he became the Lightspeed Rescue Red Ranger.

The emergency services gimmick makes the Rangers feel like essential members of their community, with responsibilities that extend beyond defeating monsters. Rescue vehicles, an underwater headquarters, and organized support staff give the heroes a convincing working environment, while it remains undeniably a Power Rangers story thanks to demons bringing danger their technology can’t always deal with. Plus, Ryan Mitchell (Rhett Fisher), the Titanium Ranger, adds an endearing redemption story and an original Ranger identity created specifically for the American series. It’s a satisfying blend of professionalism and supernatural adventure that few other Power Rangers shows can match.

In a recent development, there is an infectious enthusiasm to Power Rangers Dino Charge that makes it almost feel like a love-letter to everything that came before. Its dinosaur powers, colorful alien threats, and expanding Ranger lineup turn the search for the Energems into a lively and gripping adventure. Beginning on Nickelodeon in 2015 under Saban and continuing with Power Rangers Dino Super Charge in 2016, Dino Charge brought a welcome dose of energy and enthusiasm to the franchise. The team feels genuinely enthusastic about being Rangers, and that excitement gives viewers plenty of reasons to follow their adventures.

In a recent development, the unusual backgrounds of the Rangers in Dino Charge makes it especially endearing compared to many other Power Rangers highlights. Koda (Yoshi Sudarso) is a prehistoric human adjusting to modern life, while Ivan (Davi Santos) brings a medieval knight’s sense of honor into the group. At its core, Dino Charge is beloved because it has a team of Rangers fans are just as happy to spend time with out of costume as they are watching battle. That character-focused approach gives its increasingly elaborate adventures a human center, turning what could have been yet another dinosaur season into a team adventure with a particularly generous supply of personality.

Few Ranger teams are as immediately comfortable in their own firm as the central trio in Power Rangers Ninja Storm. Shane Clarke (Pua Magasiva), Tori Hanson (Sally Martin), and Dustin Brooks (Glenn McMillan) have an easygoing and authentic chemistry that makes their friendship convincing before their training produces dependable heroes. When their ninja academy is attacked, the three students find themselvs as its unlikely defenders. Their mistakes are part of the attraction, giving their eventual competence a satisfying foundation in shared experience and growing trust.

The 2003 Power Rangers season launched the franchise’s New Zealand production era under Disney with a noticeably playful identity. Extreme sports, elemental ninja abilities, and enthusiastic comedy give it a distinctive flavor. However, it knows when to get serious too, with arcs like the emergence of the Thunder Rangers complicating the team’s playful dynamic. That balance of breezy entertainment and meaningful progression ensures Ninja Storm continues to be considered a highpoint by the Power Rangers fandom.

According to recent reports, terra Venture gives the Power Rangers Lost Galaxy team something unusually tangible to protect: an entire traveling community attempting to build a future among the stars. The 1999 Saban season combines its science fiction premise with ancient swords and living animal Zords, creating a distinct identity that, decades later, feels like one of the best representations of what makes Power Rangers’ style of storytelling so unique. However, that’s not the greatest creative achievement of Lost Galaxy. The core of why this Power Rangers series endures is that its Rangers share their journey with the inhabitants of Terra Venture, for whom danger is an ever-present aspect of daily life.

Every major setback threatens something much bigger than the outcome of the next battle, and the colony’s vulnerability gives the Rangers’ responsibilities a deep emotional grounding. What’s more, Lost Galaxy doesn’t hold back from exploring some of the darker implications of its dangerous premise. Kendrix Morgan (Valerie Vernon) sacrifices herself to save others, while Leo Corbett (Danny Slavin) grows into his leadership role through a series of incredibly difficult decisions. Meanwhile, central villain Trakeena (Amy Miller) was among the most ruthless villains Power Rangers had seen up to that point. Few shows in the franchise explored what heroism actually demands like Lost Galaxy, and it deserves every bit of love the fandom still has for it.

The 2009 season immediately stood out because humanity had already lost most of the world when Power Rangers RPM begins. Survivors shelter in Corinth while the computer virus Venjix (Andrew Laing) controls the wasteland outside, giving the Rangers an unusually desperate assignment. The Rangers aren’t here to save the world, they’re here to protect what little remains of it. The final fresh season of Disney’s ownership, RPM builds an absorbing story around the people carrying that burden. Doctor K (Olivia Tennet) is especially memorable: her incredibly well-written, guarded behavior born of a painful history gives the team’s technical expert a depth beyond creating upgrades.

Of course, Power Rangers isn’t Power Rangers if it’s incredibly bleak, and it's impressive how confidently RPM manages to retain a sense of light-hearted adventure and the franchise’s token comedy despite the setting being one of darkest the show’s ever seen. The friendship and interpersonal drama of the Rangers helps Power Rangers RPM keep the atmosphere of the wider franchise without losing its own unique identity. The combination of the season’s ruined world with its exceptionally well-written characters and its masterful tonal balancing act secured RPM’s place as a Power Rangers show fans have been returning to time and time again for over a decade and a half.

Teamwork is at the heart of the appeal of Power Rangers, but every fan knows that this aspect works best when it's earned after the Rangers have to overcome personal differences. Few seasons pulled this off as well as Power Rangers S.P.D., whose Rangers Jack Landors (Brandon Jay McLaren) and Sky Tate (Chris Violette) gave the franchise one of its most satisfying friction-laden story arcs. One arrives with natural leadership instincts and an unconventional background, the other believes his discipline and training should put him in command. Their struggle to respect one another counts for some of the franchise’s best character drama, with the S.P.D. team having to learn to become an effective unit by reconsidering their individual ideas of what a leader should be.

This interpersonal tension works even better thanks to S.P.D. having one of the most distinctive Power Rangers settings. Released in 2005 and set in 2025, S.P.D. imagines humans and aliens sharing Earth, with Space Patrol Delta defending them from criminal threats and invasion while supported by an entertaining ensemble of characters like Commander Anubis Cruger (John Tui). Its futuristic world is enjoyable on its own, but the team’s gradual growth makes spending time there rewarding for reasons beyond the unique sci-fi trappings.

In a recent development, bringing Tommy Oliver (Jason David Frank) back as a mentor figure was an inspired way to connect Power Rangers Dino Thunder with the franchise’s beginnings. The 2004 Disney season didn’t just feature Tommy as a nostalgia-grabbing cameo, either. His experience as a veteran Ranger was necessary to guide three very different students as they discover dinosaur powers and learn to become the Morphin Grid’s next generation of heroes. His presence made the world of Power Rangers feel continuous in ways it hadn’t for years, with the younger Rangers ensuring the energy and sense of adventure at the core of the franchise remained intact.

Recent findings suggest that dino Thunder also boasts some of the most satisfying character arcs of any Power Rangers season before or since. For example, Trent Fernandez-Mercer (Jeffrey Parazzo) has a White Ranger storyline that masterfully ties into Tommy’s own history. Meanwhile, central villain Mesogog (Latham Gaines) gives Dino Thunder’s take on the already-done dinosaur theme a sinister edge that distinguishes it from previous prehistorically-rooted Ranger stories. The result has both the accessibility of a fresh beginning and the satisfaction of an established universe. It gave longtime viewers meaningful continuity while introducing a Ranger team worth following in their own right, a feat few versions of Power Rangers have managed.

No Power Rangers show rests on the shoulders of a single character, but it’s impossible to ignore how much Pink Ranger Jen Scotts (Erin Cahill) gives Power Rangers Time Force an exceptionally strong emotional center. Her determination, grief, and gradual acceptance of the burden of authority make her one of the franchise’s most compelling leadership figures. What’s more, her developing relationship with Wes Collins (Jason Faunt) gives the season a romance with genuine dramatic weight that’s rarely seen in the franchise. The 2001 Saban series sends officers from the year 3000 into the present to pursue escaped mutant criminals. That premise may seem straightforward, but Time Force uses it as a foundation for some deeply emotional storytelling.

Jen, Wes, and the other Time Force Rangers regularly find themselves having to decide whether the futures laid out for them are worth protecting from change, and what changing those futures might cost the people they love. This underlying existential tension is supported by some of the most well-written and rounded characters in Power Rangers history. Eric Myers (Daniel Southworth) brings resentment and class tension to his rivalry with Wes, while Ransik (Vernon Wells) makes prejudice a central theme of Time Force’s villain arc. Understanding his anger never means excusing what he does with it, but it’s much more satisfying than an antagonist whose goal is taking over the world for no discernible reason beyond wanting to conquer it.

While it aired almost 30 years ago, the two-part finale of Power Rangers in Space, “Countdown to Destruction,” was a game-changing moment for the franchise. Power Rangers had flirted with serialized narratives in its earlier seasons, but in Space finally unlocked their full potential. Released in 1998 during the original Saban era, it sends the Rangers beyond Earth to search for their captured mentor and confront an expanding alliance of villains. The cosmic scale was unlike anything there’d been in the franchise up until that point. Not only did the show manage to pull off this huge shift in scope, but it managed to do so with a level of success that even future space-based Power Rangers seasons haven’t really matched.

Power Rangers in Space pulled off something spectacular by making the franchise’s interconnected universe feel emotionally coherent. The villains like Astronema (Melody Perkins) and The Psycho Rangers remain fan-favorites too, both because of their aesthetic and because of how genuinely threatening they felt compared to the foes prior versions of the Rangers had faced. The true masterstroke, though, was that Power Rangers in Space never lost sight of the people at the heart of the story no matter how vast the adventure grew. That combination gives its conclusion an exceptional impact that still resonates with fans today. Years of colorful adventure culminated in choices and sacrifices that still define Power Rangers at its best.

In a recent development, it feels almost cliché to say that the first Power Rangers season remains its most beloved, but that doesn’t make it any less true. The franchise may have grown considerably since Mighty Morphin Power Rangers, but many fans still consider it the apex of everything that keeps them committed to the Rangers and their adventures. Launching in 1993, MMPR turned teenagers, martial arts, dinosaur machines, and gloriously theatrical monsters into an irresistible identity. Its original team made heroism feel inseparable from friendship and a shared desire to do good.

It has been revealed that that wholesome energy remains central to the franchise’s appeal years later, and nowhere does it feel purer and less distilled than in the Mighty Morphin era. The martial arts action is intense, the Zords make the moments that teamwork culminates in victory feel spectacular, and the Rangers’ civilian lives in Angel Grove make it feel like a home worth defending. However, the story had a lot of emotional depth to it too, especially during arcs like Tommy Oliver’s journey from Rita Repulsa’s evil Green Ranger to becoming the White Ranger and leading the team. Power Rangers has always been built on the idea that ordinary people can become extraordinary when they work together, and no iteration feels like it delivers on this enduring ideal quite like MMPR.

Crowe is many years removed from his years as an Oscar contender, but back at the start of the 2000s, one could make the case that he was the hottest actor on the planet. He was also nominated the following year for A Beautiful Mind.

The film was directed by Padraic McKinley, who has also been tapped to direct the fresh Sicario movie that’s being written by Steven Knight (Peaky Blinders).

Check out The Weight on Prime Video and stay tuned to Collider for more updates and coverage of Russell Crowe’s future projects.

This Note-Taking Pebble Ring Is so Simple, and I Love It

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Pebble’s $75 ring, the Index 01, has one job: It lets you record voice memos.
  • According to recent reports, in this era where every tech product is trying to also be every other tech product, I appreciate the Index’s simplicity.
  • To buy the Index 01 ring, you get yourself a sizing kit (either buy one for $10 or 3D print it yourself), order the ring, and pair it with the Pebble app on your phone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pebble’s $75 ring, the Index 01, has one job: It lets you record voice memos. That seems like it would be underwhelming, and the idea was ridiculed by some of Pebble’s fans when the product was first declared. But I’ve been wearing it for a few weeks, and folks: I love it.

According to recent reports, in this era where every tech product is trying to also be every other tech product, I appreciate the Index’s simplicity. This is a ring with no heart rate sensors or even charging pins, just a microphone, a button to activate it, and a light to let you know that it’s working. The audio is processed on your device; no need to send anything to the cloud.

To buy the Index 01 ring, you get yourself a sizing kit (either buy one for $10 or 3D print it yourself), order the ring, and pair it with the Pebble app on your phone. I use an iPhone rather than an Android, which means I can’t use certain features like setting timed reminders or connecting to Beeper, but it’s still an incredibly useful little device. The Index has no charger, since it uses a disposable battery that Pebble estimates will last about two years.

Industry observers note that the simplest way to use the Index is to wear it on your index finger (hence the name, get it?) and press the button with your thumb. Speak a quick note while holding the button in, and the ring will flash to let you know it got the message. A moment later, you’ll get a notification saying that it added (whatever you noted) to your “Notes to self” note.

To take this further, you can create different notes and ask the ring to add what you say to a specific note. You can also double-click the button to ask a question. The answer will appear in the notification you get on your phone or watch a moment later. (The ring does not speak to you.).

Sources indicate that all the notes you leave yourself appear as plain text in the Pebble app, fully editable. If you tap on each one, you can see a timestamp from when you left the note, and you can replay the voice recording if the transcription doesn’t make sense. (Why is there a “pencil sharp pepper” on my packing list? Ohh, that’s a pencil sharpener.) You can also add notes by typing them, which I find useful when starting a to-do list or a packing list.

In a recent development, it’s incredible how useful a simple timestamped note can be. I used to do something similar with my “notes to self” chat in Signal, but the Index makes it even easier since I won’t get distracted by opening my phone. For example, I make a note on the Index whenever I take a medication, so that tomorrow morning I will be able to check whether I already took, say, a long-acting allergy pill. (You do not want to accidentally double up on those.).

In a recent development, there’s one thing that, for years, I wished for a simple tool to help me do. It’s trivial, which makes it extra frustrating that I have not been able to find a good solution. I would simply like to note when I leave for a road trip, and when I start and end each stop. This way I can tell how long the driving took as a portion of the whole trip, and how long my stops tend to be so I can plan them better next time.

You’d think this would be easy, but every existing tool drove me nuts in a different way. Stopwatches only store a single number, so I can’t break down how long each stop was—and if I miss a button press, I’m screwed. Sending myself a Signal text is probably my best option, but if I’ve just parked my car after three hours of driving, the second I pick up my phone I’m going to see all the notifications that arrived while I was on the road, and I’ll forget to actually send that text.

Industry observers note that but this is exactly what the Index does well. I don’t even need to open my phone or look at my watch. Pressing the button with my thumb means I can do this one-handed without having a microphone always listening. (It’s also a great way to jot down the random things I think of while driving.).

According to recent reports, the Index worked perfectly for my travel log, and I even used it for a workout after I got to my hotel room that night. I’d do 10 pushups, then tell the ring “add 10 pushups to my workout.” I’d do 20 crunches, and add that as well. I left the workout note open on my phone and could glance over and see what I had already done, since my messages got added to the note as I went.

It has been revealed that I didn’t need a workout app for any of this, or a special-purpose travel app. I can just leave myself a dang note, and the note-taking app can remember when I left the note and, if I choose, play back exactly how I stated it. It’s gloriously simple. Good job, Pebble.

It has been revealed that the Rings of Power took a while to find its feet, but each season has improved on the last. The show had a monumental task ahead, further expanding J.R.R. Tolkien's high fantasy masterpiece without using material from his other works. Tolkien's estate has only permitted adaptations of The Lord of the Rings and The Hobbit, so The Rings of Power has used the books' appendices to go deep into the history of Middle Earth and explore a character who is central to both movie trilogies, but despite shaping the fate of the world, is never truly seen.

People who have only seen Peter Jackson's The Lord of the Rings movie trilogy saw Sauron briefly in armor but mostly know him as The Great Eye, watching from the tower of Barad-dûr and communicating in the language of Mordor. However, while he is briefly mentioned in The Hobbit book as "the Necromancer," the movies expanded on this role. Now, The Rings of Power is showcasing this ability. Seeing Sauron's journey from master craftsman to The Dark Lord onscreen is, at last, winning audiences over, with The Rings of Power's third season getting its highest Rotten Tomatoes audience score yet.

Sauron's stealth introduction as Halbrand was an unusual decision that instantly added intrigue to The Rings of Power, but it was not necessarily popular with fans. The Lord of the Rings is one of the greatest high fantasy stories ever written, and is told through character studies and an epic scale rather than a mystery box format. Still, the show appeared to learn from this initially polarizing setup and explore Sauron as a character with motivations and skills in the second season, which revealed his extraordinary talent as a blacksmith.

The three seasons of The Rings of Power.

Rotten Tomatoes critics' rating.

Rotten Tomatoes audience rating.

As we know that The Rings of Power will eventually cover how Sauron created The One Ring, setting up this ability through his blacksmithing now feels like his backstory is being filled out, instead of being told through confusing exposition. Sauron's motivations and desire to shape the world according to his will are explored through this creative talent, and the way his skills parallel his view of the world act as much better character building. This is now paying off, with season 3 revealing the much more sinister magic that we know he has.

Sauron's shocking necromancy scene in which he reveals the truth about Theo's father gives viewers a glimpse of his potential. Not only does he appear to act as a messenger for Theo's dead father, Fäldred, but he uses the information he is given to manipulate Theo into taking one of the Rings of Power. The question of Theo's eventual identity is still being debated, but it is possible that we have just seen Sauron create the Witch-king of Angmar. With his dark magic scenes bringing his talents for creation and corruption together, Sauron is now entering a fresh phase.

In a recent development, sauron goes through several names in Tolkien's Middle Earth saga, and while it is not possible to put an exact year on The Rings of Power due to time jumps and compressing Tolkien's histories, season 3 takes place in the middle of the Second Age, with the character honing his manipulation skills. However, his dominant set of talents in the third season foreshadow his Third Age name, "The Necromancer of Dol Guldur." Mirkwood might still be known as Greenwood in The Rings of Power, but Dol Guldur has already made an appearance, though it is not yet Sauron's stronghold.

According to recent reports, the events in the Third Age occur long after the current Rings of Power storyline, suggesting that there may be a significant time jump, or the story will end before the Third Age begins, potentially leaving room for more of the story to be told through a different series. This could take the franchise into true horror territory, with Sauron channeling necromancy and corrupting his surroundings. The exact timeline for The Rings of Power has not yet been revealed, but with two more seasons to go, this was the turning point where the blacksmith became the necromancer.

According to recent reports, set in the Second Age of Middle-earth, The Rings of Power explores the forging of the iconic rings, the rise of the Dark Lord Sauron, and the epic events leading up to the stories in J.R.R. Tolkien's classic novels.

#109212. 7 Best Video Games Based on Books, Ranked

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1913 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Collider ↗ Open Full Page

7 Best Video Games Based on Books, Ranked

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1913 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that literature and gaming are vastly different media.
  • Industry observers note that from fun shooters like Spec Ops: The Line to RPG masterpieces like The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt, these are games which show how to turn a great book into an equally great—or perhaps even better—gaming experience.
  • Industry observers note that the first-ever winner of the Japan Horror Novel Award was Hideaki Sena's sci-fi horror novel Parasite Eve, one of the best Japanese speculative fiction books of the '90s.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that literature and gaming are vastly different media. Whereas books rely on very fixed plots, internal monologues, pacing wholly controlled by the author, and the constraints of the printed page, games are all about player agency, repeatable mechanics, and complex interactive systems. However, there have been seven particularly exceptional games throughout history which prove beyond a shadow of a doubt that it's perfectly possible to make an incredible game based on a book. When these two forms of storytelling overlap, it often results in absolutely fascinating experiences.

Industry observers note that from fun shooters like Spec Ops: The Line to RPG masterpieces like The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt, these are games which show how to turn a great book into an equally great—or perhaps even better—gaming experience. Where books excel at building fascinating worlds that the reader wants to get lost inside, games actually do allow players to immerse themselves into such worlds in ways that literature simply can't match. These adaptations show that, when crafted by a strong enough developer, games can actually complement the literary medium in all sorts of interesting ways.

Industry observers note that the first-ever winner of the Japan Horror Novel Award was Hideaki Sena's sci-fi horror novel Parasite Eve, one of the best Japanese speculative fiction books of the '90s. It was adapted into a film in 1997 and a manga series in 1998, and after that came the eponymous video game developed and published by Square. It's actually a sequel to the novel, following NYPD officer Aya Brea as she hunts down a rogue entity named Eve across six days in Manhattan to stop monstrous mutations. This RPG was Square's first M-rated game, and it was part of a major revitalization of J-horror sparked by Sena's original book.

There are those who would go so far as to say that the best installment of the bunch is the game.

Recent findings suggest that the game itself also received a manga adaptation, but there are those who would go so far as to say that the best installment of the bunch is the game. For one, the concept of taking a novel and making a video game sequel is pure creative bliss, a highly ambitious endeavor that Square definitely succeeded at. The writing is great, including a lot of profound character work and terrifying lore, but the level of player agency that's directly tied to the title's RPG mechanics is also worthy of applause. Is the game perfect? No, since its pacing and rough-around-the-edges PS1 mechanics haven't aged the best; but combine great writing with some deeply atmospheric gameplay, and you get one of the most underappreciated horror games of the '90s.

Sources indicate that joseph Conrad's 1899 novella Heart of Darkness is still one of the most universally acclaimed novellas ever written, a game-changing modernist masterpiece whose razor-sharp critique of European colonialism and imperialism was far ahead of its time. The book has been adapted a few times throughout history (perhaps most notably by Francis Ford Coppola in the form of Apocalypse Now), including one of the best war video game masterpieces of all time: Yager Development and 2K's Spec Ops: The Line, where a Delta Force squad enters a sandstorm-buried Dubai to find a rogue colonel and evacuate survivors.

Industry observers note that the way The Line weaponizes video game conventions to achieve the same psychological effect that Conrad conveyed with prose alone is absolutely admirable, proof that it's perfectly possible for a video game adaptation of a book to live up to its legendary source material. Where Heart of Darkness critiqued 19th-century European imperialism, The Line critiques the modern military institution just as scathingly. Far from just playing out like a by-the-numbers third-person military shooter, the game subverts the heroic power fantasy of the genre and depicts psychological collapse with tremendous complexity and nuance.

Industry observers note that tom Clancy is a titan of modern thriller fiction, having helped define the techno-thriller genre with The Hunt for Red October and the rest of his iconic Ryanverse series of books. It's hard to think of other authors who turned their names into such massive multi-media entertainment brands. Video games soon became a part of that franchise, starting with the 1987 game adaptation of Hunt for Red October. In 1998, Red Storm Entertainment published a tactical shooter video game based on Clancy's novel Rainbow Six, thus kickstarting the franchise of the same name, which is perhaps the video game series most often associated with Clancy's name. The story follows Rainbow, a top secret international counterterrorist organization.

Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six didn't actually adapt Rainbow Six after the fact; rather, Clancy wrote the novel at the exact same time that his own studio, Red Storm, was coding the game. Released three weeks after the novel, the game practically invented the tactical shooter genre by transporting Clancy's obsession with procedural realism directly into its gameplay loop. Where many '90s shooters were fast-paced one-man-army power fantasies, Rainbow Six revolutionized the genre by making planning every bit as notable as shooting. Many of the game's mechanics have become a bit clunky over time, but it's still a must-play.

Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor isn't actually a direct adaptation of J. R. R. Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings, nor any other of his Middle-earth books; but it's an inventive and loving rendition of the world Tolkien created in his Legendarium. It's one of the best high fantasy video games of all time, following a Gondorian ranger who's revived by the wraith of the Elf Lord Celebrimbor. He invades Mordor to avenge his murdered family, while helping the spirit recover its lost memories and strike back at Sauron. For anyone who loves any kind of Middle-earth media, it's an absolute must-play; and even for people who love high fantasy gaming but have never actually read Tolkien or watched any of the movies, it's still very much worth picking up even 12 years after its initial launch.

The game bends Tolkien's lore and themes in some pretty major ways, which may drive Legendarium purists away.

It's true that the game bends Tolkien's lore and themes in some pretty major ways, which may drive Legendarium purists away, but the title's strengths are far too many and far too large to ignore. The massive standout here is Monolith Productions' proprietary Nemesis System, a gem mechanic that procedurally generates unique enemies who remember past encounters with the player, evolving over time. But even aside from that masterful mechanic, Shadow of Mordor has plenty to offer. The combat is fluid and brutal, the stealth and parkour are fun, and the richly atmospheric Mordor is an absolutely enrapturing world to operate within as this character.

Inspired by the first Fallout game and the books of Roger Zelazny and Ray Bradbury, Russian author Dmitry Glukhovsky delivered in 2002's Metro 2033 one of the most engaging post-apocalyptic novels of the 2000s. Years before he was even offered a publishing deal, he uploaded the novel's manuscript to his personal website, leading several game studios to approach him for a potential adaptation. Glukhovsky, honored by the idea, chose Ukrainian studio 4A games, trusting that they would understand the source material's thematic relation to the fall of the Soviet Union.

Sources indicate that the result of such a collaboration was 2010's Metro 2033, a survival horror and first-person shooter masterpiece unlike anything else that the 2010s had to offer. Glukhovsky gave the studio full freedom to do whatever they wanted with the material, and with a special amount of focus on story and atmosphere, 4A lifted the book's oppressive sense of dread and boosted it with challenging resource management, complicated moral choices, and gripping shooting mechanics. From beginning to end, Metro 2033 is a masterclass in how to turn literary density into fully interactive action.

Recent findings suggest that ukrainian game developer GSC Game World turned Arkady and Boris Strugatsky's philosophical sci-fi novel Roadside Picnic and turned it into the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. franchise, one of the best first-person shooter survival horror franchises in gaming history. Soviet filmmaker Andrei Tarkovsky had adapted the novel back in 1979 and turned it into one of the best soft sci-fi movie masterpieces in history, but GSC delivered something entirely different. As much of a masterpiece as the first installment in the series, Shadow of Chernobyl, is, it's arguably the fourth title in the series, S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2: Heart of Chornobyl, that's the best of the bunch.

Sources indicate that following a stalker entering an anomaly-filled Zone to recharge a mysterious artifact that destroyed his home, Heart of Chernobyl is one of the most atmospheric, immersive, and entertaining first-person shooters of the 2020s so far. Though it's not a direct adaptation of the plot of the Strugatskys' book, it's still a phenomenal adaptation that reimagines the book's setting by maximizing its horrific sense of atmosphere. The survival gameplay is enrapturing, the shooting mechanics are butter-smooth, and the environmental storytelling is masterful.

Sources indicate that with The Last Wish, the world was introduced to Polish author Andrzej Sapkowski's The Witcher book series. For years, the novels remained popular mostly just in Eastern Europe, and it wasn't until CD Projekt Red made the 2007's RPG video game adaptation of the same title that the whole Witcher IP became a household name. The franchise reached its peak in 2015 with The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt, where the monster hunter Geralt of Rivia traverses a war-torn world to find his adopter daughter before the spectral Wild Hunt captures and exploits her.

It's easily one of the best fantasy video games for beginners, one of the few modern RPG action-adventure titles that can genuinely be stated to be absolutely perfect. It's a sequel set after Sapkowski's book saga ends, and that narrative freedom allowed the developers to really go all-out with their imagination, making the absolute bast of the foundations laid out by the source material's lore, narrative, and characters. The depth of the character writing is tremendous, the world is so large and cohesive that it's impossible to ever grow tired of exploring it, and the gameplay is some of the most entertaining that fantasy gaming has seen in years. As far as video game adaptations of books go, it doesn't get any better than this.

It has been revealed that four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

In a recent development, you would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

#109211. Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

📅 09 Feb 2022 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2893 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The AI pioneer says it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to significant challenges.
  • Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.
  • According to recent reports, andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The AI pioneer says it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to significant challenges.

Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.

According to recent reports, andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence. He pioneered the use of graphics processing units (GPUs) to train deep learning models in the late 2000s with his students at Stanford University, cofounded Google Brain in 2011, and then served for three years as chief scientist for Baidu, where he helped build the Chinese tech giant’s AI group. So when he says he has identified the next big shift in artificial intelligence, people listen. And that’s what he told IEEE Spectrum in an exclusive Q&A.

Industry observers note that ng’s current efforts are focused on his organization Landing AI, which built a platform called LandingLens to help manufacturers improve visual inspection with computer vision. He has also become something of an evangelist for what he calls the data-centric AI movement, which he claims can yield “small data” solutions to big concerns in AI, including model efficiency, accuracy, and bias.

According to recent reports, the great advances in deep learning over the past decade or so have been powered by ever-bigger models crunching ever-bigger amounts of data. Some people argue that that’s an unsustainable trajectory. Do you agree that it can’t go on that way?

It has been revealed that andrew Ng: This is a big question. We’ve seen foundation models in NLP [natural language processing]. I’m excited about NLP models getting even bigger, and also about the potential of building foundation models in computer vision. I think there’s lots of signal to still be exploited in video: We have not been able to build foundation models yet for video because of compute bandwidth and the cost of processing video, as opposed to tokenized text. So I think that this engine of scaling up deep learning algorithms, which has been running for something like 15 years now, still has steam in it. Having mentioned that, it only applies to certain problems, and there’s a set of other problems that need small data solutions.

When you say you want a foundation model for computer vision, what do you mean by that?

It has been revealed that ng: This is a term coined by Percy Liang and some of my friends at Stanford to refer to very large models, trained on very large data sets, that can be tuned for specific applications. For example, GPT-3 is an example of a foundation model [for NLP]. Foundation models offer a lot of promise as a new paradigm in developing machine learning applications, but also challenges in terms of making sure that they’re reasonably fair and free from bias, especially if many of us will be building on top of them.

What needs to happen for someone to build a foundation model for video?

Ng: I think there is a scalability problem. The compute power needed to process the large volume of images for video is significant, and I think that’s why foundation models have arisen first in NLP. Many researchers are working on this, and I think we’re seeing early signs of such models being developed in computer vision. But I’m confident that if a semiconductor maker gave us 10 times more processor power, we could easily find 10 times more video to build such models for vision.

Recent findings suggest that having remarked that, a lot of what’s happened over the past decade is that deep learning has happened in consumer-facing companies that have large user bases, sometimes billions of people, and therefore very large data sets. While that paradigm of machine learning has driven a lot of economic value in consumer software, I find that that recipe of scale doesn’t work for other industries.

It’s funny to hear you say that, because your early work was at a consumer-facing firm with millions of consumers.

Ng: Over a decade ago, when I proposed starting the Google Brain project to use Google’s compute infrastructure to build very large neural networks, it was a controversial step. One very senior person pulled me aside and warned me that starting Google Brain would be bad for my career. I think he felt that the action couldn’t just be in scaling up, and that I should instead focus on architecture innovation.

Sources indicate that “In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from major data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.” —Andrew Ng, CEO & Founder, Landing AI.

Industry observers note that I remember when my students and I published the first NeurIPS workshop paper advocating using CUDA, a platform for processing on GPUs, for deep learning—a different senior person in AI sat me down and said, “CUDA is really complicated to program. As a programming paradigm, this seems like too much work.” I did manage to convince him; the other person I did not convince.

I expect they’re both convinced now.

Over the past year as I’ve been speaking to people about the data-centric AI movement, I’ve been getting flashbacks to when I was speaking to people about deep learning and scalability 10 or 15 years ago. In the past year, I’ve been getting the same mix of “there’s nothing new here” and “this seems like the wrong direction.”.

How do you define data-centric AI, and why do you consider it a movement?

Industry observers note that ng: Data-centric AI is the discipline of systematically engineering the data needed to successfully build an AI system. For an AI system, you have to implement some algorithm, say a neural network, in code and then train it on your data set. The dominant paradigm over the last decade was to download the data set while you focus on improving the code. Thanks to that paradigm, over the last decade deep learning networks have improved significantly, to the point where for a lot of applications the code—the neural network architecture—is basically a solved problem. So for many practical applications, it’s now more productive to hold the neural network architecture fixed, and instead find ways to improve the data.

When I started speaking about this, there were many practitioners who, completely appropriately, raised their hands and stated, “Yes, we’ve been doing this for 20 years.” This is the time to take the things that some individuals have been doing intuitively and make it a systematic engineering discipline.

The data-centric AI movement is much bigger than one manufacturer or group of researchers. My collaborators and I organized a data-centric AI workshop at NeurIPS, and I was really delighted at the number of authors and presenters that indicated up.

According to recent reports, you often talk about companies or institutions that have only a small amount of data to work with. How can data-centric AI help them?

Industry observers note that ng: You hear a lot about vision systems built with millions of images—I once built a face recognition system using 350 million images. Architectures built for hundreds of millions of images don’t work with only 50 images. But it turns out, if you have 50 really good examples, you can build something valuable, like a defect-inspection system. In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from substantial data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.

When you talk about training a model with just 50 images, does that really mean you’re taking an existing model that was trained on a very large data set and fine-tuning it? Or do you mean a brand new model that’s designed to learn only from that small data set?

It has been revealed that ng: Let me describe what Landing AI does. When doing visual inspection for manufacturers, we often use our own flavor of RetinaNet. It is a pretrained model. Having said that, the pretraining is a small piece of the puzzle. What’s a bigger piece of the puzzle is providing tools that enable the manufacturer to pick the right set of images [to use for fine-tuning] and label them in a consistent way. There’s a very practical problem we’ve seen spanning vision, NLP, and speech, where even human annotators don’t agree on the appropriate label. For big data applications, the common response has been: If the data is noisy, let’s just get a lot of data and the algorithm will average over it. But if you can develop tools that flag where the data’s inconsistent and give you a very targeted way to improve the consistency of the data, that turns out to be a more efficient way to get a high-performing system.

“Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.” —Andrew Ng.

For example, if you have 10,000 images where 30 images are of one class, and those 30 images are labeled inconsistently, one of the things we do is build tools to draw your attention to the subset of data that’s inconsistent. So you can very rapidly relabel those images to be more consistent, and this leads to improvement in performance.

Could this focus on high-quality data help with bias in data sets? If you’re able to curate the data more before training?

In a recent development, ng: Very much so. Many researchers have pointed out that biased data is one factor among many leading to biased systems. There have been many thoughtful efforts to engineer the data. At the NeurIPS workshop, Olga Russakovsky gave a really nice talk on this. At the main NeurIPS conference, I also really enjoyed Mary Gray’s presentation, which touched on how data-centric AI is one piece of the solution, but not the entire solution. Fresh tools like Datasheets for Datasets also seem like an key piece of the puzzle.

One of the powerful tools that data-centric AI gives us is the ability to engineer a subset of the data. Imagine training a machine-learning system and finding that its performance is okay for most of the data set, but its performance is biased for just a subset of the data. If you try to change the whole neural network architecture to improve the performance on just that subset, it’s quite difficult. But if you can engineer a subset of the data you can address the problem in a much more targeted way.

When you talk about engineering the data, what do you mean exactly?

Ng: In AI, data cleaning is notable, but the way the data has been cleaned has often been in very manual ways. In computer vision, someone may visualize images through a Jupyter notebook and maybe spot the problem, and maybe fix it. But I’m excited about tools that allow you to have a very large data set, tools that draw your attention rapidly and efficiently to the subset of data where, say, the labels are noisy. Or to quickly bring your attention to the one class among 100 classes where it would benefit you to collect more data. Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.

For example, I once figured out that a speech-recognition system was performing poorly when there was car noise in the background. Knowing that allowed me to collect more data with car noise in the background, rather than trying to collect more data for everything, which would have been expensive and slow.

What about using synthetic data, is that often a good solution?

Recent findings suggest that ng: I think synthetic data is an important tool in the tool chest of data-centric AI. At the NeurIPS workshop, Anima Anandkumar gave a great talk that touched on synthetic data. I think there are important uses of synthetic data that go beyond just being a preprocessing step for increasing the data set for a learning algorithm. I’d love to see more tools to let developers use synthetic data generation as part of the closed loop of iterative machine learning development.

Do you mean that synthetic data would allow you to try the model on more data sets?

According to recent reports, ng: Not really. Here’s an example. Let’s say you’re trying to detect defects in a smartphone casing. There are many different types of defects on smartphones. It could be a scratch, a dent, pit marks, discoloration of the material, other types of blemishes. If you train the model and then find through error analysis that it’s doing well overall but it’s performing poorly on pit marks, then synthetic data generation allows you to address the problem in a more targeted way. You could generate more data just for the pit-mark category.

Sources indicate that “In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion customers. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models.” —Andrew Ng.

Synthetic data generation is a very powerful tool, but there are many simpler tools that I will often try first. Such as data augmentation, improving labeling consistency, or just asking a factory to collect more data.

To make these concerns more concrete, can you walk me through an example? When a organization approaches Landing AI and indicates it has a problem with visual inspection, how do you onboard them and work toward deployment?

Industry observers note that ng: When a customer approaches us we usually have a conversation about their inspection problem and look at a few images to verify that the problem is feasible with computer vision. Assuming it is, we ask them to upload the data to the LandingLens platform. We often advise them on the methodology of data-centric AI and help them label the data.

According to recent reports, one of the foci of Landing AI is to empower manufacturing companies to do the machine learning work themselves. A lot of our work is making sure the software is fast and easy to use. Through the iterative process of machine learning development, we advise customers on things like how to train models on the platform, when and how to improve the labeling of data so the performance of the model improves. Our training and software supports them all the way through deploying the trained model to an edge device in the factory.

How do you deal with changing needs? If products change or lighting conditions change in the factory, can the model keep up?

In a recent development, ng: It varies by manufacturer. There is data drift in many contexts. But there are some manufacturers that have been running the same manufacturing line for 20 years now with few changes, so they don’t expect changes in the next five years. Those stable environments make things easier. For other manufacturers, we provide tools to flag when there’s a significant data-drift glitch. I find it really important to empower manufacturing customers to correct data, retrain, and revision the model. Because if something changes and it’s 3 a.m. in the United States, I want them to be able to adapt their learning algorithm right away to maintain operations.

In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models. The challenge is, how do you do that without Landing AI having to hire 10,000 machine learning specialists?

So you’re saying that to make it scale, you have to empower customers to do a lot of the training and other work.

Industry observers note that ng: Yes, exactly! This is an industry-wide problem in AI, not just in manufacturing. Look at health care. Every hospital has its own slightly different format for electronic health records. How can every hospital train its own custom AI model? Expecting every hospital’s IT personnel to invent upcoming neural-network architectures is unrealistic. The only way out of this dilemma is to build tools that empower the customers to build their own models by giving them tools to engineer the data and express their domain knowledge. That’s what Landing AI is executing in computer vision, and the field of AI needs other teams to execute this in other domains.

Is there anything else you think it’s key for people to understand about the work you’re doing or the data-centric AI movement?

Ng: In the last decade, the biggest shift in AI was a shift to deep learning. I think it’s quite possible that in this decade the biggest shift will be to data-centric AI. With the maturity of today’s neural network architectures, I think for a lot of the practical applications the bottleneck will be whether we can efficiently get the data we need to develop systems that work well. The data-centric AI movement has tremendous energy and momentum across the whole community. I hope more researchers and developers will jump in and work on it.

This article appears in the April 2022 print matter as “Andrew Ng, AI Minimalist.”.

According to recent reports, popular secure messaging app Signal has rolled out a new patch that automatically disables screenshots for the sake of blocking Siri AI from reading your chats. Here are the details.

Signal’s latest app revision on iPhone disables a key system feature: taking screenshots.

As Signal told Reuters, that’s because Apple doesn’t currently provide better tools for iOS developers to safeguard app content from Siri AI and third-party AI agents.

By default, users who revision and try to take a screenshot will see a message that says: “Screenshot prevented by ‘Block Siri AI’ setting.”.

Fortunately, there’s an easy workaround. Users who want to re-enable screenshots can do so by visiting Signal’s privacy settings and turning off the latest toggle that’s labeled ‘Block Siri AI.’.

Here’s 9to5Mac’s own Arin Waichulis:.

Signal now blocks in-app screenshots on iPhone to keep Siri AI from reading chatsIt’s a latest toggle in settings that’s on by default, but can be turned offNo equivalent for its Mac app pic.twitter.com/ImsinqMNPq.

Here’s exactly what that toggle does, per the in-app settings:.

It has been revealed that prevent Siri AI from scanning Signal content. This will also block you from taking screenshots in the app and App Switcher.

According to recent reports, it’s good to see that users can manually disable the latest privacy setting if they want. But Signal’s decision to block screenshots does raise important questions about the potential gap in privacy tools for iOS developers.

Apple already lets you block Siri AI from accessing whichever apps you manually exclude, and that became even easier in iOS 27.2. But rather than directing consumers to that system option, Signal seems to believe it needed to take action itself with this update.

Tech Report: Gemini Notebook's New Interactive Site Builder Is Much More Useful Than I Expected

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (968 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, gemini Notebook, Google's AI tool for study and research, already lets you do a lot with your notes: You can turn them into flashcard quizzes, interactive podcasts, video explainers, mind maps, and infographics, as well as interrogating the sources you've collected through AI-powered prompts and responses.
  • It has been revealed that that might not immediately seem like the most obvious fit, turning your research notes into a mass of HTML code.
  • Website building is rolling out now for Gemini Notebook's web app for all users, and is "coming soon" to the mobile app.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, gemini Notebook, Google's AI tool for study and research, already lets you do a lot with your notes: You can turn them into flashcard quizzes, interactive podcasts, video explainers, mind maps, and infographics, as well as interrogating the sources you've collected through AI-powered prompts and responses. Now there's something upcoming. You can also build interactive websites from your notebooks.

It has been revealed that that might not immediately seem like the most obvious fit, turning your research notes into a mass of HTML code. But it gives you another way to look at your material and to get insights from it. Here's how it works, what you could potentially do with it, and how impressively it worked when I put it to the test on some early 20th-century Irish literature.

Website building is rolling out now for Gemini Notebook's web app for all users, and is "coming soon" to the mobile app. You won't see a website option in the Studio panel alongside Audio Overview, Reports, Quiz, and the rest; instead, you type something along the lines of "make me a website" in the prompt box.

Industry observers note that to make a website, you need sources, so I set Gemini Notebook to collect information about James Joyce's 1914 collection of short stories, Dubliners. As I studied Dubliners many years ago (I highly recommend it), I was hoping I'd spot any AI errors and hallucinations, and be able to properly assess the quality of Gemini Notebook's analysis.

Recent findings suggest that with a suitable amount of information absorbed into the AI brain, I got Gemini Notebook to make me a website. Google doesn't give too much official guidance here, but claims you should add "a description of what you want to build for work or study," so if you have a particular style or angle in mind, include it.

According to recent reports, here was my prompt: "Build a website using all the sources and information collected so far. Make it an interactive guide to the individual stories in Dubliners, as well as the overarching themes and context. I want to use it as a study aid to explore different aspects of the story collection.".

It has been revealed that the finished website pops up in the Studio panel, and in my case it took around five minutes to put something together from 26 different sources. Click on the website, and it opens in a new window—you can use it from there, open it in a separate tab, or download the code to your computer.

I was honestly impressed by how much Gemini Notebook managed to pack into a single website: I got plot summaries, analysis, critical context, and some of the main themes and motifs outlined. There was an interactive quiz at the bottom of the page to test my knowledge, and even a graphic I could click through to reveal different elements of how the stories fit together.

Everything was well laid out and functional, albeit with the standard "sheen" you get from anything made by AI (which tends to always pick the same colors and fonts). I wouldn't have necessarily thought that I needed a website if I was still studying Dubliners today, but I can definitely see how it would have helped.

Industry observers note that for something like my project, a website really works well as a study aid, since it offers a different way of interrogating the information. You can already do that in the main chat, and with tools such as the audio and video overviews, but this is different. It's a bit like having a mini-Wikipedia focused just on whatever you're researching.

The interactive elements that are included—so in my example, I could click from story to story, and theme to theme, within the same page—make a site more engaging than a standard report document and a static wall of text, and should help the information stick if you're trying to study it.

Sources indicate that I can also see how this might be useful for sharing data with others. Maybe you need to analyze monthly report figures, or you want to chart how your organization has developed a product over time—perhaps an interactive website will relay that information in a more compelling way than a slide deck or PDF.

Maybe you have a notebook stuffed with details of a significant family vacation. Putting together a website through Gemini Notebook would give your family a hub that they could use to easily check up on the details of the trip—where you're going and when, what you'll see there, what they need to pack, and so on. Another idea might be a family tree, if you have ancestry data and sources packed together in a notebook. Putting together a website would be a great way to visualize it, and, again, it's something you could share with relatives. If there were updates to the data you've collected, you could generate a latest website.

Industry observers note that bear in mind that you can do a lot with your prompt. My website turned out the way it did because that's what I asked for, and if you need more interactivity or specific types of sections, then you can ask. Based on my follow-up prompts, you can also specify colors and certain layout choices, though it's not quite a full-scale website builder.

It looks like these sites are single-page creations, though they do have interactive elements and sections that change as you click around. It might be better to think of them as mini apps rather than sites. As of yet, there's no built-in option for publishing a site online or sharing it with others, so you need to download the HTML and do that manually.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • 2026 is the year of the horror genre!
  • This year, numerous small-budget features also left a lasting impression.
  • We follow socially awkward Bear Bailey (Michael Johnston), consumed by infatuation with his longtime crush, Nikki (Inde Navarrette).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

2026 is the year of the horror genre! Early in the year, 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple set the tone for genre fans with its sincere twist on the infected’s origins; then Sam Raimi’s return to genre with Send Help gave fans a dark comedic twist, and with franchise sequels like Scream 7, Scary Movie, and Insidious: Out of the Further, fans returned to familiar territory.

This year, numerous small-budget features also left a lasting impression. Kane Parsons’ Backrooms adapted the viral liminal-space horror to fans’ satisfaction and pulled in over $400 million worldwide on a meager $10 million budget. Then there’s YouTuber-turned-director Curry Baker’s Obsession. It is hands down the breakout supernatural psychological horror of the year, rising to become a massive cultural phenomenon and worldwide sensation, let alone becoming one of the most financially successful movies ever made.

We follow socially awkward Bear Bailey (Michael Johnston), consumed by infatuation with his longtime crush, Nikki (Inde Navarrette). Unable to express his feelings, Bear breaks open a novelty trinket called the "One Wish Willow" and wishes for Nikki to love him more than anything else in the world. It works instantly, transforming Nikki into an intensely devoted partner. Things take a turn when her affection rapidly escalates into erratic, violent, and even lethal behavior. As bodies pile up, Bear realizes Nikki’s true consciousness is trapped inside her own body, forcing him to confront the horrifying cost of reversing the wish.

The film took off with younger audiences, who related to the themes of abusive relationship dynamics and coercive control. The film explores the toxic “nice guy” entitlement, exposing how seemingly harmless infatuation can curdle into selfishness and emotional coercion. The loss of autonomy and consent is reflected in Nikki’s real self being trapped inside her own body. And the narrative mostly warns the audience to be careful about what you wish for.

With its thematic relevance and a gripping narrative, Obsession became a breakout hit, earning $286 million worldwide on a $750,000 budget. Further, it received wide praise for Navarrette’s brilliant performance, where she balances manic devotion with flashes of trapped terror, while Johnston was praised for capturing Bear's shift from pathetic to monstrous. After enchanting audiences in theatres, Obsession is now casting a spell on streaming services. The feature has spent over 185 days on Apple TV Store’s global top 10 charts. It has also spent over 140 days on Prime Video.

Check out Obsession on Apple TV Store or Prime Video. Stay tuned to Collider for more updates.

💡 Key Takeaways
