Industry observers note that the Acer Predator Connect T7 is a mesh Wi-Fi system with a heavy focus on gamers. However, unlike my previous mesh router pick for gaming, the Asus ROG Rapture GT6, it’s a Wi-Fi 7-powered device with a much more subtle look.

In a recent development, instead of RGB and lots of logos, the Predator Connect T7 features a taller, rectangular design in white or black, and at first glance, it looks quite similar to an Xbox Series X. There’s a splash of RGB lighting on the top, but this mesh kit has a sleeker and more restrained look that I think definitely works in its favor.

Recent findings suggest that just like with the best gaming routers, the Predator Connect T7 has a low-latency design that uses Intel’s Killer Prioritization engine for peak gaming performance. It also comes with free built-in security software and makes full use of all of Wi-Fi 7’s best features.

According to recent reports, during testing, Brian saw download speeds of 1.9 Gbps at close range (15 feet) with good mid-range performance. While the Predator Connect T7 has a multi-gig input port, its wired Ethernet ports are limited to gigabit speeds, so plugging in one of the best gaming laptops won’t give you a significant speed boost over connecting via Wi-Fi.

The Acer Predator Connect T7 is one of the few mesh Wi-Fi systems specifically designed for gamers and if you want a mesh router that looks as slick as your gaming PC, it’s a big step up from the Asus ROG Rapture GT7 (which superseded the GT6 we used to recommend).

However, it is on the expensive side at $330 per device, and unlike other mesh kits, you won’t see any discounts at all when buying a multi-pack. Still, if you want gaming-level network performance with the added benefits of mesh and want something less flashy, the Predator Connect T7 is an excellent mesh Wi-Fi system and the only one for gamers with Wi-Fi 7 support so far.

The Eero Pro 7 is a smaller and sleeker mesh Wi-Fi system that’s incredibly simple to set up and use. Unlike Eero’s past mesh kits, which had a puck-shaped design, this one has a rounded rectangular shape and, at 7.1 x 5.8 x 2.6 inches, you won’t have any trouble finding a place for it and its satellites around your home.

It has been revealed that after testing the larger, more powerful Eero Max 7 myself, I really like the Pro 7’s more compact design and the fact that it's significantly cheaper, too. The biggest selling point of the Pro 7 and Eero’s other mesh Wi-Fi systems is that even a home networking novice will have no trouble at all getting them up and running.

Setup and configuration are handled entirely through the very user-friendly Eero app. Besides how it looks, I really like the way that updates are downloaded and installed automatically, so your mesh Wi-Fi system is always running the latest software.

In his testing, Brian saw download speeds of 1.9 Gbps at close distances (15 feet), but the Pro 7 was equally impressive at mid-range distances with speeds just under a gigabit.

The Eero Pro 7 does cost a bit more than the competition, but nowhere close to what you’d pay for an Orbi mesh kit. As an Amazon manufacturer, Eero works great with your Alexa-powered and other smart home devices, and you can even use an Echo Dot as a mesh extender to add some extra range to your home network.

If you want a fast and capable Wi-Fi 7-powered mesh system that’s simple to set up and just works, the Eero Pro 7 is very easy to recommend, especially since it's a lot cheaper than the Max 7. The one downside is that you’re limited to just two Ethernet ports, but they are the faster 5 Gbps variety, which is great if you have a multi-gig internet strategy.

Industry observers note that the TP-Link Deco BE85 is a top-of-the-line mesh Wi-Fi system that was actually the first mesh router with Wi-Fi 7 support. It builds on the cylindrical design of the Deco XE75 with a more refined and polished look, but it packs in a ton of multi-gig and even a USB port.

As someone who upgraded to fiber internet, I love how it has its own SFP+ port, which lets you plug your fiber line directly in at the back instead of into a separate ONT box first. Even if you’re still using one of the best cable modems, though, the Deco BE85 is a powerful mesh Wi-Fi system that won’t disappoint when it comes to performance.

Sources indicate that one thing that’s really convenient about this mesh kit and TP-Link’s other Deco devices is that they’re all identical out of the box and you can use any of them as your main router. The company’s Deco app also makes setup and configuration very easy, and in my experience, it’s on par with Eero’s app in terms of usability.

15 feet (Toms Guide): TP-Link Deco BE85 scores 1.736.

50 feet (Toms Guide): TP-Link Deco BE85 scores 790.4.

75 feet (Toms Guide): TP-Link Deco BE85 scores 179.2.

90 feet (Toms Guide): TP-Link Deco BE85 scores 42.6.

Recent findings suggest that during testing, Brian saw download speeds of 1.73 Gbps at a close distance (15 feet) and good mid-range speeds, too. While this might seem a bit low for a premium mesh Wi-Fi system, Brian was one of the first people to get and review the Deco BE85. It's possible this has improved with firmware updates since its launch.

In a recent development, the Deco BE85 has come down in price since it launched, but it’s still expensive, even though this model does go on sale quite frequently. However, if you have a fast, multi-gig fiber internet blueprint and want top-notch Wi-Fi 7 performance, this mesh router is the only one I’ve seen yet with an SFP+ port on the back.

It’s worth noting that, just like with Eero, all TP-Link Deco devices are compatible with one another, so you could always mix and match or upgrade to a more powerful model later on if you need to.

Sources indicate that the mesh Wi-Fi systems we've used all come with amazing speeds, and we've done the testing to show how fast a router is at short and long ranges. But you'll find some will perform better at various distances, even if one delivers the fastest speeds around.

As an example, the Acer Predator Connect T7 offers the fastest speeds at 15 feet, but it loses out to the likes of the TP-Link Deco BE23 and others at 90 feet. It comes down to what you prioritize: speed or range (or a balance of both!).

So, to compare each mesh Wi-Fi system across the range of distances we've tested, check out the versus table below to help you make the right choice for your home.

Select a mesh Wi-Fi system to compare internet speed at different distances (measured in Gbps and Mbps).

We test every mesh Wi-Fi system to measure performance and range, using Keysight IxChariot. Testing is done in a multi-story home with brick walls. When we test standard routers, we look at performance at a distance to provide real-world information about coverage and speeds. In addition to lab testing, we evaluate the ease of setup and features of each device, too.

Sources indicate that we measure performance at a 15-foot distance without obstructions, so that we can gauge the maximum amount of data that a router can move. Higher throughput will serve you better in data-heavy uses, like streaming video, gaming, or connecting multiple owners at once.

Range measures the furthest usable distance for a particular router. Longer ranges are better for larger homes, where rooms are spread out at a distance. We measure how much data a router can move at 15, 50, 75 and 90 feet, as well as the maximum coverage area of a mesh Wi-Fi system.

We also test how well each mesh Wi-Fi system transmits and receives signals through drywall, brick, concrete and even metal walls, and how each handles coverage in a two- or three-story home. They also go through additional testing to see how well each system does when sending a signal through the main router and through the included satellites.

Of course (and most importantly), we also consider what you really get for your money, considering which features are worthwhile and how any given product compares with other devices from competing manufacturers.

A lot of factors come into choosing the mesh Wi-Fi system that will suit your space, from the coverage you need to the speeds you demand — all for the right price. We've got just the tips to make your choice easier.

It has been revealed that wi-Fi 8 is currently still in the early stages of being supported on all devices, so you won't be able to take advantage of the latest connectivity standard right now. Currently, no consumer devices support Wi-Fi 8 coverage, and we're not expecting to see support until sometime in 2027 or 2028.

Sources indicate that we've reviewed the first Wi-Fi 8 router, the Asus ROG Rapture GT-BN98 Pro, and are impressed by its incredible Wi-Fi speeds and range. However, we couldn't see its full potential since we're still waiting for Wi-Fi 8 hardware. We'll have to see how well mesh Wi-Fi systems with Wi-Fi 8 perform, too.

It has been revealed that while Wi-Fi 8 isn't worth getting right now, it may be worth it to many looking to future-proof their homes once more devices adopt Wi-Fi 8. Besides, it's backwards compatible with Wi-Fi 7, Wi-Fi 6 and so on. We'll keep you updated in the meantime.

Sources indicate that yes, a mesh Wi-Fi system can go through walls. Because Wi-Fi uses radio waves, these waves can pass through solid materials like walls to connect to a device.

However, when Wi-Fi meets a wall, some of it goes through, some bounces off and some is absorbed. Because of this, the signal can be weaker, especially when more walls are in the way.

Industry observers note that A mesh Wi-Fi system has an advantage in getting past this. Instead of using one router to get a signal, a mesh system uses multiple nodes placed throughout a home to bypass hard objects or walls in order to get an unobstructed signal. This means there are fewer barriers to getting a clear Wi-Fi signal.

In a recent development, the main downside of using a mesh Wi-Fi system is that it can be very expensive, especially compared to traditional Wi-Fi routers. These are only needed for those living in large homes or for anyone who needs Wi-Fi coverage over a long distance. For those in smaller spaces, this is overkill.

Since mesh systems come in a multi-pack of nodes, this bumps up the price, as these extra devices deliver a better range of coverage throughout a space compared to other routers.

Industry observers note that nodes also must be placed close enough to catch a strong signal, which can be tricky in a home with many rooms separated by concrete or brick walls. Plus, with this signal hopping between multiple nodes, there may be an increase in latency, which isn't ideal for competitive gameplay.

Otherwise, the best mesh Wi-Fi systems try to overcome these downsides, and these are still the best option to upgrade your home network wirelessly.

Recent findings suggest that mesh Wi-Fi systems come with nodes and are usually available in two-packs or three-packs, but deciding which one to get depends on the size of your home. If you live in a small or medium house, then a two-pack will usually do the trick. For large homes with more than three bedrooms or multiple stories, a three-pack is the better choice, as this will ensure that your Wi-Fi signal reaches every corner and even upstairs.

In a recent development, the great thing about mesh Wi-Fi systems, though, is that you can always start small and work up to something bigger. For instance, if you buy a two-pack and find that you’re still dealing with Wi-Fi dead zones in certain parts of your home, you can always add another node later to improve your coverage.

According to recent reports, plug-in Wi-Fi extenders aren’t nearly as advanced or as powerful as the nodes in a mesh Wi-Fi system. The other substantial problem with Wi-Fi extenders is that most of them create a separate network you have to manually switch to each time you want to use them. For instance, let’s say you put a Wi-Fi extender in your bedroom. Whenever you want to get online in that particular room, you’ll have to switch from your main Wi-Fi network to the extender, which gets annoying really fast.

According to recent reports, on the other hand, with a mesh Wi-Fi system, the nodes are all part of your main network and no switching is required. As you move from one side of your house to the other, your mesh system automatically hands off your connection to whatever satellite you’re closest to, which ensures you have a strong signal and a good connection wherever you are in your home.

Sources indicate that as someone who's been working from home for the past eight years, Anthony Spadafora has tried everything from Wi-Fi extenders to powerline adapters to get the most out of his home network, before finally upgrading to a mesh Wi-Fi system. Along the way, he's tested out loads of different routers and network configurations. Based on what he's learned, Anthony tries to highlight the critical role Wi-Fi routers play in our day-to-day lives and how a mesh network can help solve the most common connectivity concerns like Wi-Fi dead spots.

With experience in testing, using and evaluating wireless data from before Wi-Fi was even a word, Brian Nadel has tried out and reviewed every major router available in his home networking lab. A LAN nerd, his philosophy is to use the router the way you would, testing networking gear for ease of setup, performance, security and above all for value. The result is peace of mind when it comes to choosing the right router.

Will Siri AI threaten Apple’s environmental target, given Google and Meta admissions?

💡 Key Takeaways

  • All of this could potentially be put at risk by the manufacturer’s ambitions for Siri AI, however, as Meta joins Google in admitting it is now unlikely to meet its own 2030 net zero promise, thanks to the huge power demands of the data centers powering its AI services ….
  • In a recent development, apple’s environmental record isn’t entirely perfect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, I think Apple can reasonably claim to be the leading tech giant when it comes to its environmental credentials. It has led the way with its use of renewable energy, made significant strides with carbon-neutral production, and removed plastic from all its packaging.

All of this could potentially be put at risk by the manufacturer’s ambitions for Siri AI, however, as Meta joins Google in admitting it is now unlikely to meet its own 2030 net zero promise, thanks to the huge power demands of the data centers powering its AI services ….

In a recent development, apple’s environmental record isn’t entirely perfect. For example, when it claimed that the Apple Watch Series 9 and Ultra 2 were carbon neutral back in 2023, that claim was described as “bogus,” with the EU banning Apple from repeating it. The company has also been criticized for pushing a relentless annual iPhone cycle, encouraging frequent upgrades.

Recent findings suggest that overall, however, Apple has first-rate credentials when it comes to the environment. It was way back in 2018 when the firm hit its goal of running its own operations off 100% renewable energy. This includes all Apple facilities, from Apple Park through data centers to its worldwide retail store network.

I said at the time that using more environmentally friendly packaging should be the company’s next priority, and it has indeed made great progress with this over the years, succeeding in removing all plastic packaging earlier this year.

After its own operations, Apple set about trying to tackle the power usage of its manufacturing partners. Back in 2020, the company set a goal of having its entire supply chain be carbon neutral by 2030. Just four years later, Apple said it was 95% of the way there.

The company also helps fund and support a wide range of environmental initiatives around the world. Just a few examples include conservation in China’s national parks, environmental protection and carbon removal in Australia and Upcoming Zealand, and helping to fund the build-out of renewable energy capacity in India.

In a recent development, potentially, however, the vast energy demands of the data centers powering AI services could put its 2030 goal at risk. Other tech giants have already admitted that it may lead them to fail to hit their own renewable energy promises.

It has been revealed that back in 2024, for example, Google CEO Sundar Pichai stated that the AI boom was “challenging” to the organization’s 2030 carbon-free goal. CNET reports that Meta is now also admitting that it may fail to hit the same target.

Meta’s data center and sustainability chiefs wrote that the company is “re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones — including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets.” In an emailed statement to CNET, a Meta spokesperson added, “We remain committed to net zero, but are re-evaluating the 2030 timeline.”.

Notably, a lot of Siri’s most advanced AI capabilities are currently powered by Google’s Gemini models.

Industry observers note that at the same 2024 event where Google expressed doubts, Apple reiterated its commitment to its 2030 target. Then-CEO Tim Cook repeated this assurance later the same year, although admitted it would be challenging.

According to recent reports, more challenges, yes. But are we coming off the goal? No, definitely not. With more data centers, you use more renewable energy, and we’ve built that muscle now […] I feel very good about 2030.

In the company’s most recent environmental progress report, it stated that it was was still using 100% renewable energy despite using over 2.5 billion kWh of electricity to power its data centers.

We’re proud that 100 percent of that electricity came from renewable sources including solar, wind, and low-impact hydropower. To cover our needs, we build our own renewable power projects and work with utilities to purchase clean energy from locally obtained resources. We’re staying at 100 percent even as Apple’s data center capacity continues to grow.

The same report remarked the company had achieved zero water use for cooling at its latest data centers.

At our three newest data centers, we use high-efficiency air-cooled chillers instead of water-cooled systems, resulting in zero water use for cooling.

However, the greatest challenge for Apple lies ahead. The reason that Google and Meta are now backtracking on their promises is that both companies now have massive AI capabilities. As yet, Apple does not.

What happens as Apple expands Siri AI capabilities as usage increases, and as the company moves into agentic AI features? Is it realistic for the company to maintain its 100% track record with vastly greater data center energy usage?

Greenpeace expressed its own doubts earlier this year.

In a recent development, “AI will be the defining test of Apple’s climate commitments,” spokesperson Avex Li says. “To preserve Tim Cook’s environmental legacy, the manufacturer will need to show that AI growth can be accommodated within its existing climate commitments through absolute emissions reductions, additional renewable energy investment, and longer-lasting products.”.

Apple did not respond directly but merely pointed to its past statements and most recent environmental progress report.

I don’t doubt the tech giant’s desire to maintain its track record, but if Apple does join the likes of Google and Meta in becoming a major AI player, sticking to its 2030 timing is going to become increasingly difficult.

In a recent development, do you think Apple will succeed? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • I've been playing Grand Theft Auto VI since launch, and I'm having a blast so far.
  • I'm not going to share any spoilers here, but you should know that the side quests in Chapter 1 are crucial.
  • Sources indicate that if you're used to playing racing games, you'll find the driving experience in GTA VI to be quite different.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I've been playing Grand Theft Auto VI since launch, and I'm having a blast so far. The world feels even more detailed and immersive than previous GTA games, which means there's a lot to learn beyond the basic tutorials and prompts the game shares at the beginning. These are the 10 GTA 6 hacks I used to improve the game's quality of life. If you do the same, you'll spend more time immersed in the world, and less time fighting the game's default settings.

I'm not going to share any spoilers here, but you should know that the side quests in Chapter 1 are crucial. If you ignore all the optional quests or small asks by other characters, you won't be able to return to those later. These are small things like fixing up the house for Lucia, meditating with her, and buying her a necklace when she asks you to. All of these have an impact on your progress. Take your time in this chapter, and remember to save before starting the mission called "Recalibration." That mission leads to Tourist Trap, which is the point of no return for Chapter 1.

Sources indicate that if you're used to playing racing games, you'll find the driving experience in GTA VI to be quite different. It's hard to keep an eye on minimap directions while you're also getting used to vehicles in the game, and I used voice navigation to ensure that I don't keep getting lost, particularly for time-sensitive missions. You can enable this by going to GTA VI settings > Audio > GPS Voice > Voice. If you're playing the game on PS5, your DualSense controller's speaker plays GPS voice prompts. This is great as those alerts can be hard to hear over all other in-game sounds from your TV's speaker.

Using GTA 6's default controls, making Jason and Lucia run is quite annoying. The game makes you hold L3 to run, which hurts my thumbs. If you alter movement speed in settings, you can make the characters run just by using the left stick. You can walk by easing off the left stick, or switch to a fast walk, jog, or run when you push the stick all the way. Tweak this by going to GTA VI settings > Gameplay > Movement Speed > Jog. This lets you move faster without draining your stamina. You can also change from Jog to Run if you want the fastest possible movement speed with the left stick. Having remarked that, my pro tip is to go to Control Scheme in settings, and switch to Classic. This lets you run by holding the X button, as opposed to L3 with default controls.

It has been revealed that haptic strength is one area where GTA 6 takes the immersion a bit too far, as it's dialed up to the maximum level by default. This makes the controller's vibration strength a bit too intense for my liking, and also has a negative impact on battery life. You can fix that by reducing haptic strength a little. It's under GTA VI settings > Controller > Vibration & Haptics Strength.

Many modern controllers develop "stick drift," an issue where small movements of the analog sticks register as large inputs. This causes a massive problem in games that require precise inputs, such as GTA 6. To counter this potential problem, the game allows you to adjust the deadzone for each analog stick in your controller. That said, this setting can be used to your advantage, even if you don't have stick drift complications in your controller. I recommend dialing up the deadzone to 7 to improve the driving experience. I find most cars in GTA 6 to be a bit floaty to drive, and adjusting the deadzone fixes this issue to a large extent.

Sources indicate that committing a heist attracts heat in GTA 6, and there are many different ways to escape the attention of in-game cops. The usual tricks include stocking up on outfits to change into, parking your vehicle a block or two away, and being so stealthy that you leave no witnesses to your crimes. However, an underrated trick involves using the pickup truck you get at the start of the game. Get a bike in the game, and stash it in your pickup truck. Then, use the truck to drive to the crime scene, and hide the truck a short distance away. Unload the bike, and use it to get to the crime scene. Once the heist is complete, ditch the bike, and run to your truck. Witnesses won't have seen you using the truck, which allows you to escape the area promptly.

It has been revealed that if you are using a car as a getaway vehicle, you can use two tricks to make a smooth escape. First, double-tap the Triangle button to exit your vehicle without switching off its engine. When you return to the vehicle in a hurry, you can escape a lot faster. If you have quick fingers, you can double-tap Triangle first, and just as your character is about to exit the vehicle, press L3 (or X, if you use classic controls). This leaves the car's door open, and saves you a little more time when you're fleeing.

Recent findings suggest that I suffer from chronic migraines, and I am sensitive to bright lights. Fortunately, GTA 6 has a bunch of accessibility settings that help me play the game for longer. Even if you don't face the same issues, these settings will help reduce eye strain in longer play sessions. Go to GTA VI settings > Display > Flashbang, and switch to Dark. This stops flashbangs from showing a bright white light when they go off. On the same settings page, you can tweak Player Status Effects Intensity to reduce screen effects when your character is low on health or stamina. You can also enable Brightness Reduction to reduce the intensity of bright lights in the game, and try Focus Trail Colorblind Mode if you find it hard to distinguish between different colors.

According to recent reports, I haven't been able to play first-person shooters for decades because the camera movement makes me nauseous and gives me a headache. Of late, I've noticed that it's getting harder to play third-person games too. My first two hours in GTA 6 had me quite worried because I was feeling quite sick, and I had to turn off my PS5. Luckily for me, I found a few tweaks to mitigate this problem. You can do that in GTA VI settings > UI > Persistent Center Dot. This permanently demonstrates a white dot in the center of the screen, and it reduced my motion sickness enough to help me play the game. You can also go to GTA VI settings > Camera, reduce Camera Bob, and turn off Camera Shake, and Weapon Sway. I also recommend going to the Controller tab in settings, and tweaking all the options under Aim & Look Sensitivity until you find a comfortable level.

GTA 6 includes realistic ringing sounds that linger after explosions in the game. This may be fine for some people, but it can negatively affect some players' gaming sessions. Those who suffer from tinnitus or chronic migraines may not enjoy those ringing sounds, and, luckily, the game allows you to disable them. Open GTA 6's in-game settings, and enable the feature from Audio > Tinnitus Reduction.

#109103. Worshipping at the altar of Brendan Gregg

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1420 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fzakaria ↗ Open Full Page

Worshipping at the altar of Brendan Gregg

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1420 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fzakaria

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, okay, I am the first to admit that I’m a bit manic with AI.
  • Recent findings suggest that I have been amazed at all the fun and useful things that a deterministic VM like Rewind enables.
  • Turns out that performance is yet another area where Rewind shines.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, okay, I am the first to admit that I’m a bit manic with AI. When you are working on a problem that has endless possibilities, it is difficult to constrain yourself to a limited set of features.

Recent findings suggest that I have been amazed at all the fun and useful things that a deterministic VM like Rewind enables. I have been using it to help find heisenbugs, to make profile-guided optimization reproducible, and to make Nix builds bit-reproducible. But the most fun has been using it to understand performance.

Turns out that performance is yet another area where Rewind shines. I have been using it to analyze the critical path of builds.

The critical path is the longest chain of dependent work in a program. It is the minimum time that the program can take to complete, regardless of how many resources you throw at it. The only way to make a program faster is to shorten the critical path.

Sources indicate that if you worship at the altar of Brendan Gregg, you know he spent years turning performance analysis from a dark art into a science. This is a small offering to him. 🤲.

Industry observers note that I added a newly introduced rewind time command to Rewind that analyzes a recording and tells you where the time went and what would make the run finish sooner. You can drill into any part of that answer and see the source lines responsible for it. It’s like Brendan Gregg’s flame graphs but on steroids for the critical path and with a debugger attached.11All the ideas for the command are either inspired by or directly influenced by Brendan Gregg’s work. Kneel before Zod!

In a recent development, aside: Newly introduced to Rewind? Start with a flaky build you only catch once and dafuq is a deterministic VM?

Let’s see how it works by analyzing the critical path of a libuv build and test run. The build and test suite takes 78 seconds inside Rewind, and even with 64 cores it still takes 47 seconds. Why?

According to recent reports, the usual answer is to look at a CPU profile, and in this case a CPU profile would be almost useless. For two thirds of those 47 seconds, the work the build is waiting on is not computing at all: it is asleep. 💤💤💤.

Every rewind time starts with two numbers:.

It has been revealed that the first is how long the run took on the VM’s one virtual CPU. The second is the critical path: the longest chain of work where each step had to wait for the one before.

No number of CPUs makes a run shorter than its critical path, so the gap between the two numbers is all that parallelism can buy you.

The line under the two numbers applies Gregg’s thread state analysis. Here the biggest state is asleep: 23 seconds in epoll_pwait and 8.5 in clock_nanosleep.

In a recent development, A sleeping thread is invisible to a CPU profiler. Gregg’s answer is off-CPU analysis: look at where threads block, not only where they compute.

Industry observers note that on a live machine, off-CPU analysis is hard. Linux can trace which thread woke which, and Gregg built wakeup and off-wake profiling on top of that, but you have to be tracing before the slow run happens, the tracing has a cost, and most of the sleeps you capture are noise. Rewind already logs every context switch because it needs them to replay, and now it records every wakeup and who caused it too. All that juicy information is in every recording. 🤤.

Here is the whole output for libuv:.

The second table is the path as a tree of processes based on Gregg’s colony graph idea. Each line is a process with everything it started, and its time on the critical path.22A ps snapshot might miss short-lived process invocations; the recording has every fork, regardless of how brief.

In a recent development, in this build, make check needs 41.9 of the total 47.4 seconds, and 36.4 of that is lt-run-tests, libuv’s test runner. The test runner invokes 287 tests each spending 1-3 seconds.

It has been revealed that all of those tests are on the path, and the path is a single chain, so the runner ran them one after another. Worse, most of each test is spent asleep, waiting on timers.

Drag can be less than time on the path.

In a recent development, the last table answers a different question: how much sooner would the run finish if this part took no time? The critical path method calls this drag.

For the truly magical part, we can jump to any part of the path and see what was happening, invoke gdb and fork the run at that moment. A profiler hands you a stack, sampled at some moment you can never go back to. Every frame in rewind time is a moment in a recording, and Rewind can replay the run to it.

Recent findings suggest that --in looks inside one process,33It can take a pid, a program or a word of the command line. so let’s dive into the hrtime test that spent 3.38 seconds asleep in clock_nanosleep:.

It has been revealed that since this test spent 100% of its time asleep, the step provided on the last line is where it began. rewind where replays the run to that step and asks gdb where the thread was:.

🎯 We can see that the test is calling uv_sleep(45) from line 39 of test/test-hrtime.c, and that it is sleeping for 45 milliseconds. It does that 75 times for a total of 3.38 seconds.44Turns out that the test sleeps on purpose: it is checking how far uv_hrtime moves across a sleep. There is nothing to optimize in this case.

As the cherry on top: the run is deterministic, so step 115,894 is the same instruction every time you replay it. You can open rewind gdb at that step and investigate to your heart’s content.

According to recent reports, the Rewind app’s Time tab indicates the same answers. The path becomes a flame graph, colored the way Gregg colors his off-CPU flame graphs: computing is warm, asleep is blue, and a process shades from one to the other by how much of its time it slept.

In a recent development, clicking a frame picks it and moves the playhead there, so the build log, the process tree and the files all show that moment; clicking a process again zooms into it. When you pick a blue frame, the app replays the run to that part’s longest sleep and shows the stack where it slept:.

Under the stack, Show source opens the source panel at that moment on that thread, and Open gdb here opens gdb in a fork of the run at the sleep:.

If you’d rather use tools you already know, rewind time can emit the data in their formats: folded stacks for flamegraph.pl and speedscope, or a Perfetto trace for ui.perfetto.dev.

The flame graph below is the real flamegraph.pl output: click a frame to zoom in, or open it on its own.

Sources indicate that every idea here predates Rewind. Gregg has been drawing off-CPU and wakeup flame graphs for over a decade, and build systems have reported critical path information potentially even longer.55Bazel’s critical path analysis is a great example of this, and it has been around for years. I have been inspired by his work since I first dabbled in eBPF, back when flame graphs were latest. 🙇.

What Rewind adds is the data. Lots of it.

Rewind has that data because it can’t replay without it. On a single CPU the only thing that changes from run to run is the scheduler, so every recording already logs every context switch.

This changes the economics of performance analysis. On a live machine, you have to trace before the run, and tracing has a cost. You can only trace a few runs, and you have to pick which ones. Rewind traces every run, so you can analyze any of them later, and do so exactly.

It has just been a manic fever joy to take ideas I have admired for years, point them at a deterministic VM, and watch them work in ways that are hard or impossible on a normal machine.

Please accept rewind time as my offering at the altar of Brendan Gregg.

Latest Update: iOS 27 basically turns your iPhone and AirPods into an Apple Watch at the gym

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (872 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • GymKit has been one of Apple Watch’s smartest fitness features since it introduced in 2017.
  • With iOS 27, Apple is expanding that idea beyond Apple Watch.
  • Recent findings suggest that the setup is simple.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GymKit has been one of Apple Watch’s smartest fitness features since it introduced in 2017. Tap your watch to compatible gym equipment, and Apple Watch shares your heart rate while the machine sends back metrics like distance, incline, pace, and calories.

With iOS 27, Apple is expanding that idea beyond Apple Watch. I tested the upcoming GymKit on iPhone and AirPods Pro 3 ($149, reg. $249) experience with a GymKit-compatible treadmill. It basically gives you the Apple Watch GymKit workout tracking experience, just without the watch. This could be useful in a lot of scenarios.

Recent findings suggest that the setup is simple. I tapped my iPhone to the treadmill, picked Indoor Walk (Indoor Run is also offered), and started the workout from the treadmill. With GymKit, workout data is stored privately on iPhone and removed from the equipment.

In a recent development, once the workout started, the treadmill received heart-rate data from AirPods Pro 3. Meanwhile, the Fitness app on iPhone received the treadmill’s distance, pace, incline, and calorie data. Treadmills know details that an iPhone and AirPods can’t know on their own, especially incline and precise belt distance.

As a side note: Apple Watch has more accurate treadmill workout tracking as part of watchOS 27. GymKit remains the gold standard for accurate data, though.

GymKit also avoids two awkward gym habits. You don’t need to hold the treadmill’s metal heart-rate contacts while jogging. You also do not need to wear a Bluetooth heart-rate strap.

Sources indicate that airPods Pro 3 become the heart-rate source (and likely your podcast or music audio source as well). iPhone becomes the workout computer, which you can monitor during your workout. And the treadmill fills in the machine data while providing the surface for walking or running.

Apple has been moving more fitness features onto iPhone for years. iOS first made the Fitness app useful without Apple Watch as Apple Fitness+ leaned into iPhone as an entry point. AirPods Pro 3 pushed that further as the first AirPods with heart-rate tracking, after Apple tested the idea with Powerbeats Pro 2.

Recent findings suggest that iOS 27 brings those pieces together. GymKit on iPhone shouldn’t replace Apple Watch for people who wear one every day. Instead, it’s a great backup when your Apple Watch is dead, charging, or left at home.

It also gives iPhone and AirPods owners a taste of the Apple Watch experience, which could attract future Apple Watch customers.

In testing with iOS 27 beta 1, my Exercise ring didn’t update as I worked out without wearing Apple Watch. But after I put my watch back on, the Exercise ring caught up, and the workout appeared in Fitness with the right data.

My sample 16-minute treadmill walk indicated 0.66 miles, 65 active calories, 97 total calories, 32 feet of elevation gain, and a 115 BPM average heart rate, just like if I’d worn an Apple Watch.

Sources indicate that I had been getting the impression that gym equipment manufacturers had been abandoning GymKit support - if they ever had done so initially. I even got the impression that the majority of equipment in Apple's own onsite Gym at the Apple Park may not have supported it - at least originally.

Does Apple have a webpage listing compatible brands and models? Like they do/did for HomeKit.

What is other people perception? Any rowing machines that support it?

…checks - surprisingly it looks like Peloton do support it on their bikes.

Industry observers note that if I tried to use GymKit on iPhone without AirPods, the iPhone disconnected when the workout started because it had no heart-rate source. If I tried to start GymKit from iPhone while wearing Apple Watch, iOS pointed me back to the Workout app on Apple Watch instead, though you can continue without using the watch.

AirPods heart-rate permission also matters. You can manage it in Settings under your AirPods settings and privacy options. I had turned it off, mostly as a theoretical battery-saving move, but this test convinced me to turn it back on. AirPods Pro 3 can also work with Apple Watch to provide the best available heart-rate data.

GymKit on iPhone is one of those iOS 27 features that sounds small until it solves a real problem. If Apple Watch is your default workout tracker, it probably stays that way.

But if your watch dies or you forget it at home, iPhone plus AirPods Pro 3 can now log a treadmill workout with real heart-rate data and real treadmill metrics.

One-line review: The Canon EOS R100 is the cheapest way to get a new mirrorless interchangeable lens camera (ILC), and its excellent image quality and solid AF make it perfect for budding photographers.

People who want to take photography seriously and have lots of creative control over their shots, whether they’re printing them or sharing them on Instagram. It’s ideal for anyone wanting an upgrade from their smartphone without breaking the bank.

According to recent reports, the EOS R100 is about as affordable as mirrorless cameras get, yet still offers the essential perks of a “proper” interchangeable lens camera. It has a 24MP APS-C sensor which produces beautiful photos and 4K video. Combined with Canon’s excellent autofocus and the ability to swap lenses when creativity demands, the EOS R100 will give you everything you need to take Instagram-worthy photos.

It has been revealed that ✅ Beautiful photos: The EOS R100’s 24MP sensor produces beautiful photos with plenty of fine detail. In testing, we loved the natural colors this camera produces, rendering warm skin tones and vivid landscapes — this is Canon all over.

✅ 4K video: The EOS R100 isn’t a video camera, but will still shoot 4K at cinematic 24p, so if you want to dabble in a bit of video, you can!

Recent findings suggest that ✅ Great autofocus: Canon’s autofocus systems are legendary. And while the EOS R100 doesn’t have the brand’s very best AF with multiple detection modes (you’ll need the Canon EOS R50 for a taste of that), it still features human face and eye detection, making it great for portraiture and general use.

✅ Plenty of creative flexibility: This is one of the only cameras on the list that’ll let you change lenses (the other is the Pentax KF), which is a big deal. As you grow as a photographer, you can swap lenses to tailor the look and style of your photos.

✅ Solid build: Despite being lightweight and compact, this is a Canon camera, so you can rest assured that it’s built to a high standard and will give you many years of loyal service.

In a recent development, ❌ Fixed LCD: The EOS R100 has a fixed LCD, which makes it harder to shoot at odd angles, as you can’t articulate the display to suit. It isn’t a touchscreen either, which means you can’t tap to set focus points.

❌ Limited detection modes: As mentioned above, the EOS R100 only features human AF detection modes, so if you’re after a camera for wildlife photography, we’d recommend something with a more expansive AF system, like the EOS R50.

The EOS R100 isn’t the most feature-packed camera, but packs in a huge amount of functionality and creative flexibility given its budget price tag. If you want a cheap camera to expand your creative horizons and improve your photography, this is the best one to buy.

Industry observers note that "Simply put, I chose the EOS R100 as it's great at doing the basics and costs very little. What more do you need on a budget?".

This camera is perfect for beginners who want a DSLR to learn the basics on, but which will also grow with them — its IBIS and weather sealing will make it a good camera as you explore more genres and get more creative.

❌ Autofocus can lag: Although the camera’s autofocus is generally effective, it may occasionally experience lag. This is annoying at times when you want immediate autofocus.

❌ Not one for video: The KF only shoots video at 1080p, so it’s not a great camera for vlogging or video, which is a shame given it has effective IBIS.

Sources indicate that the Pentax KF is a great camera for budding photographers and provides great value for money. It takes great images and has an effective IBIS system, the vari-angle display is useful for shooting at different angles, and the weather-sealed body means it can go with you everywhere and not get damaged by the elements. It’s an ideal camera to both learn and grow with.

"It’s the only budget DSLR still being made, but it’s ideal for beginners learning the exposure triangle on a budget.".

One-line review: Despite its tiny stature and budget price, the DJI Neo is absolutely stuffed to the brim with features and doesn't require FAA registration.

Industry observers note that the DJI Neo is for drone novices or enthusiasts on a budget who are looking to enter the world of drone photography. For the features it offers, this drone is excellent value for money.

In a recent development, the Neo is great for those starting out in drone photography because everything is done automatically — from exposure to ISO. It’s extremely easy to fly either with your smartphone or the RC-N3 controller, and its small size makes it the perfect travel companion. The Neo is capable of shooting 4K video at 30fps and capturing 12MP stills. It has been succeeded by the DJI Neo 2, but that drone is quite a bit pricier, so we still favor the original Neo for this guide.

✅ Easy to fly: You can control the Neo either via the DJI Fly app on a smartphone or the RC-N3 controller, and both ways are straightforward. The RC-N3 comes with two detachable joysticks which are highly responsive and comfortable to use for long hours.

✅ User-friendly app: DJI's app is free to download and easy to use, while also providing lots of functionality and control.

Industry observers note that ✅ Compact and lightweight: The Neo weighs just 4.76 ounces which means you don’t need to obtain a license to fly it (but it’s still worth checking local laws before flying). This also means it’s very easy to travel with.

✅ Smooth 4K footage: The Neo shoots 4K video at 30fps or 1080P at 60fps, which is great for the price. Footage is smooth with plenty of detail, as is panning across a scene. Its f/2.8 aperture also delivers good results in moderately lit conditions.

✅ Very affordable: At under $200, this is one of the cheapest and best drones you can buy.

Sources indicate that ❌ Short flight time: On a single charge, the Neo has a flight time of just 18 minutes which is about half the time you get with DJI’s other drones. It’s worth investing in the Fly More combo which gives you two spare batteries to bump the total flying time up to 54 minutes.

When buying a cheap camera, you’re naturally going to have to sacrifice a few things. The latest and greatest cameras simply don’t come cheap. Usually, you’ll either have to accept an older model, or sacrifice features.

Sources indicate that however, you absolutely don’t have to sacrifice quality. You can pick up some great cameras for well under $100, and they aren’t just cheap crap. And that’s where we come in! This guide is designed to help you filter out the cameras that are cheap, yet still great quality and built to last.

It has been revealed that the specific features you need to look for will depend on what you’re using the camera for. If you want to take really nice photos and grow as a photographer, then you’ll want a camera with a larger sensor, decent megapixel count and good autofocus — that means you’ll need to splash out on a DSLR or mirrorless camera.

Shooting video? You’ll want 4K footage, decent stabilization and the ability to connect external microphones. A vlogging camera is ideal, or an action camera if you’ll be shooting outdoors or in extreme environments. If you’re after sky-high footage, then you’ll want a drone (and yes, you can absolutely pick up great drones without breaking the bank).

Want to print your photos? You have a few options. The high-resolution sensors in mirrorless cameras will yield the best results when printing digital images. If you want the film look, you can go for an instant camera, which will be best for immediate printing and documenting social events, or a film camera, which will produce higher quality prints but requires film to be developed.

Sources indicate that if you need a camera for travel, then it’s all about portability. You’ll want something that takes decent photos, but is small enough to fit in a pocket or backpack, and which won’t become a chore when worn around your neck.

Every single camera on this list has been through the Tom’s Guide reviews process, which means they’ve all been thoroughly tested by Tom’s Guide experts. The testing process naturally differs for the different categories of cameras — we test an action camera differently to how we test an instant camera, for example.

However, there are many things all cameras have in common. We always test how sharp the camera optics are, looking for optical distortions and image artefacts. We always evaluate how well images turn out, how detailed they are and the color accuracy of the camera. We take lots of test shots or videos with each camera, enabling us to test autofocus, exposure metering and all the extra features such as AF modes.

Naturally, we always evaluate the price of a product, test its build quality, and analyze both how easy the camera is to use and how sensibly it’s laid out. If there’s a smartphone app, we use it and evaluate how many extra features it adds, but also how user-friendly it is. We always evaluate the battery life of cameras, too.

We don’t just list the specs or features of these cameras either, and always analyze whether each of a camera’s features is good or bad, and why — that involves weighing it up against the product’s cost and competition. Throughout each review, we constantly compare each product to its rivals to help you make the most informed purchase. We’ve included links to the individual reviews for each camera within every entry, so you can get the full lowdown on each product if you want to know more.

Why spend money on even a cheap camera when you have your smartphone, right? Won't your phone take pictures just as well?

It has been revealed that that depends on the phone and indeed the camera, but generally speaking a decent dedicated camera will be able to take better photos than your smartphone. Phones have small image sensors, as there isn't much space inside a phone case for a large sensor. The iPhone 16 uses a 1/1.29-inch sensor, which is a lot smaller than the APS-C sensor used in the Canon EOS R100. A larger sensor delivers cleaner images in low light. That said, many phones these days feature larger sensors than some cameras, especially compact cameras.

Another factor is optics. Smartphones have to use small lenses — again, as space is a major consideration. Smaller lenses just can't match the sharpness and quality of larger lenses on dedicated cameras, especially those on interchangeable lens cameras (like mirrorless or DSLR bodies).

And while some smartphones offer manual controls, often these aren't truly manual. You can adjust "aperture" on an iPhone, for instance, but the phone simply applies a software-generated blur to approximate the look of a shallow depth of field at wide apertures. While this looks OK at a glance, study the image closely and you'll see mistakes and things blurred that shouldn't be. This reliance on software is repeated in other areas by your smartphone camera, and generally results in poorer image quality.

According to recent reports, and finally, there's use case. If you want to shoot film photos, or print your photos instantly, you can't do either with a smartphone alone. Using a dedicated camera is often more fun, too! There's something special about the experience of using a camera that smartphones can't quite replicate.

In a recent development, that really depends on the category of camera you need, and the definition of “cheap” changes based on noted category. If you want the best image quality or a vlogging camera, you’ll need a mirrorless camera like the EOS R100, and cheap means around the $250-$400 mark. Action cameras, expect to spend around $175 - $200 for a cheap model.

In a recent development, great instant cameras and compact cameras can easily be found for around the $100 mark, while affordable film cameras can be yours for very little more. If you want a cheap drone, you can expect to spend in the vicinity of $200.

According to recent reports, no. Or at least, not until they're sure they want to get into photography. Cheap cameras are a great way to see if you like photography (or shooting video), and whether you really want to put in the time and dedication to learn and gain experience.

According to recent reports, that's not to say you should buy the cheapest camera you can find, though, as there are many terrible cameras out there which are a total waste of money. You should buy a decent camera which will allow you to learn without breaking the bank. And that's where this guide comes in! It will help you choose a cheap camera that's also good quality.

In a recent development, on the surface, Apple's third-generation AirPods Pro are among the best ways to listen to audio on your Apple devices. The earbuds sound great: I'm not an audiophile or a headphone reviewer, but to my ears, the Pros deliver excellent sound quality, with plenty of bass and great sound separation. I frequently turn to mine when I want to pay close attention to a fresh album, or watch a show or movie with intricate sound design. Plus, like other AirPods, the Pros are great for jumping between your various Apple devices. I'm constantly switching between my iPhone, Mac, and Apple TV with mine, and they seamlessly move between each—at least, most of the time.

The noise cancellation on these AirPods is also stellar. I used to take my AirPods Max with me on planes, but lately, I've been fine with just my Pros, since the noise cancellation seemingly blocks just about as much background sound as my over-the-ear headphones. Equally great are both the transparency modes, which pump in outside sounds while you're wearing your AirPods, and Adaptive Transparency, which automatically adjusts the level of transparency based on how loud or soft your surroundings are. This is a great mode for wearing your AirPods in loud environments, so you can still hear everything without the noise becoming overwhelming. To that point, these AirPods are actually FDA-certified hearing aids.

According to recent reports, there are plenty of other features available here as well, especially if you have a compatible iPhone. AirPods Pro 3 have a built-in heart rate sensor, so you can track workouts without an Apple Watch; you can translate conversations in real time with Live Translate; "Conversation Awareness" lowers the volume of your audio and turns on transparency mode when you start speaking; and they run for eight hours on one charge with noise cancellation enabled.

Industry observers note that this isn't an in-depth list of the AirPods Pro 3's set of features. But suffice it to say, these earbuds are worth their full MSRP of $249. Splitting USB-C: USB 3 and USB 2 on one port

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1129 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Frankchiarulli

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I started building restorekit.org dongles a few months ago at the Recurse Center.
  • Recent findings suggest that the original board, the Dongle-Lite, is USB 2 only.
  • I recently learned from timo at Twocanoes that newer Macs support USB 3 speeds for recovery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I started building restorekit.org dongles a few months ago at the Recurse Center. They are small inline USB-C boards that sit between a host computer and a target mac. They set the target mac into DFUDevice Firmware Patch: Apple's lowest-level recovery mode built into the boot ROM, so even a bricked Mac can be reflashed. mode over USB-PDUSB Power Delivery: the communication protocol over the CC wire used to negotiate power, roles, and vendor-defined commands. without having to touch the target at all, and work with an open-source toolkit for restoring macs without the need for another mac.

Recent findings suggest that the original board, the Dongle-Lite, is USB 2 only. A single USB 2 hub (CH334F) connects both the dongle’s MCU and the target mac through a single cable, while a PD PHYPhysical-layer transceiver chip that encodes and decodes USB Power Delivery packets on the CC wire. (FUSB302B) sends Apple’s DFU commands on the CC line.

I recently learned from timo at Twocanoes that newer Macs support USB 3 speeds for recovery. I obviously immediately wanted to support this on the hub for faster recovery, but the problem was cost. At first I designed a “proper” USB 3 board using a GL3510 USB 3 hub and a pair of TI SuperSpeed muxes (HD3SS3220 and HD3SS3212). It basically doubled the parts count, and BOMBill of Materials: the full list of components and quantities required to assemble one board. cost, required me to increase the size of PCB to ~100 mm, and topped out at 5 Gbps transfers between host and target (USB 3.1 Gen 1).

I really didn’t want to make a board that cost more than twice the Dongle-Lite just to get USB 3 speeds.

In a recent development, so with the 2nd version Dongle-Pro, I tried a kinda crazy USB-C experiment: drop the USB 3 hub completely, keep a cheap USB 2 hub on D+/D-, and route the USB 3 SuperSpeedUSB 3.x's dedicated high-speed TX/RX differential pairs, physically separate from USB 2's D+/D- wires. lanes as a straight passthrough from host to target on the same USB-C port. The idea being that in theory the USB 3 and 2 controllers on a USB-C are completely independent, and should work simultaneously.

Since high-speed USB 3 is super prone to interference I didn’t really have a choice other than to purchase a view boards and test it out.

In a recent development, well… I just got the boards in from JLC and… THEY WORK! They establish a full 10 Gbps USB 3.2 Gen 2 connection while connecting the dongle’s USB 2 hub and MCU over the exact same port. After some aggressive cost optimization, the 10 Gbps board also ended up cheaper and smaller than the USB 2 Dongle-Lite.

Like I mentioned earlier, USB-C is not a single data bus. Inside a standard USB-C port, USB 2 and USB 3 sit on completely different sets of pins:.

Every USB-C port has two mirrored 12-pin rows: A1 through A12 on top, and B12 through B1 on the bottom, so a cable works rotated either way.

Sources indicate that this continues to the computer’s xHCIExtensible Host Controller Interface: the USB controller inside your computer that manages both USB 2 and USB 3.x root ports. controller: a single physical USB-C port is actually wired to two independent root ports: a USB 2 port and a USB 3 port.

Industry observers note that A standard USB 3 hub chip like the GL3510 is actually just two hubs in 1 package (a USB 2 hub and a USB 3 hub). On my first iteration of the Dongle-Pro, everything ran through that chip even though the dongle’s own MCU only speaks USB 2 Full Speed (12 Mbps) and has no need for the USB 3 speed.

On the Dongle-Pro v2, the two buses are split apart:.

This sounded like it would work to me on paper, but there were a few things I thought could go wrong:.

When the boards arrived, I immediately plugged one into my mac, plugged an iPhone into the target port, and inspected the bus with system_profiler SPUSBHostDataType and ioreg -p IOUSB.

Here is what macOS sees on a single physical USB-C port (AppleT8132USBXHCI@01000000):.

The raw system_profiler SPUSBHostDataType output indicates both sides active at once:.

Recent findings suggest that 0x01100000 is the USB 2 half of the physical port, and 0x01200000 is the SuperSpeed half of the same port. The iPhone enumerated straight through both passive CH9441P muxes at 10 Gb/s (USB 3.2 Gen 2), while the CH334P hub and Dongle-Pro-v2 MCU enumerate at 480 Mb/s and 12 Mb/s on D+/D-.

Splitting the bus required one interesting change in the host SDK (restorekit).

On the Dongle-Lite, whatever device you plugged into the dongle always indicated up as a child of the dongle’s hub. That made it easy to tell which target Mac belonged to which dongle when you plugged in several at once.

On the Dongle-Pro v2, that breaks whenever the target connects at USB 3. Just like iPhone@01200000 above, a SuperSpeed target bypasses the CH334P hub completely and shows up as a sibling directly on the host’s root hub.

Turns out the OS already tracks which USB 2 and USB 3 root ports share the same physical port and it exposes it directly:.

So restorekit can still know with 100% certainty which 10 Gbps device is plugged into which dongle.

I originally planned to have a Dongle-Lite and significantly more expensive USB 3 Pro, but that means having to maintain two hardware lines, so if I could cut the cost of the USB 3 version to be comparably priced to the original Dongle-Lite it felt like a no brainer.

After I removed the GL3510 USB 3 hub from the original design, I went through the rest of the board to see what else I could cut:.

Running the three BOMs against JLCPCB pricing:.

Recent findings suggest that (Parts and Extended feeder fees from JLCPCB’s catalog, excluding PCB fab and placement fees. V2 wins on fab cost too since it is 40% smaller than the Lite and 60% smaller than Pro v1, packing three boards into one 81 x 48 mm panel.).

These swaps resulted in a 72% BOM reduction from original Dongle-Pro while doubling the SuperSpeed link rate from 5 Gbps to 10 Gbps, and a 42% BOM reduction compared to the Dongle-Lite.

According to recent reports, if you are building an inline USB-C tool where your MCU only needs a slow control channel and the host just needs fast passthrough to the downstream device, you might not need a USB 3 hub. USB-C gives you two independent buses in the same port.

Next up: A flash drive with USB 3.2 Gen 2 + 2 speeds?

Industry News: These are the best noise canceling earbuds we've tested that are actually worth your money right now

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 23 min read (4563 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • True silence when you're out and about is impossible — but you can get incredibly close with some of the best noise-canceling earbuds.
  • At the moment, the best noise-canceling earbuds you can buy are the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2.
  • If they're over your budget or you need something you won't worry about losing as much, there's always the excellent CMF By Nothing Buds 2A.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

True silence when you're out and about is impossible — but you can get incredibly close with some of the best noise-canceling earbuds. Thanks to advances in active noise cancellation (ANC), they're great at keeping the noise of your commute at bay, and their in-ear design makes them super portable. But which should you buy?

At the moment, the best noise-canceling earbuds you can buy are the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2. They've got the best ANC we've ever tested, and offer a comfortable fit so that you can wear them for long periods of time. There's little more we'd ask.

If they're over your budget or you need something you won't worry about losing as much, there's always the excellent CMF By Nothing Buds 2A. They don't cost anywhere near as much, but also offer great ANC and solid sound quality.

Recent findings suggest that I maintain the site's buying guides for headphones, wireless earbuds, Bluetooth speakers, soundbars, and more. I have spent more than 20 years testing audio equipment for my own enjoyment, and was previously the Audio Editor here at Tom's Guide. There's nothing more I love than jamming out to my favorite tunes on audio equipment of different prices and sizes.

The Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2 bring improvements to the formula across the board, in all but one key area. If you were to unbox your brand-newly introduced buds next to a pair of the old model, you'd be forgiven for wondering if you'd be shortchanged.

In a recent development, they look identical. All the way down to their eartip shape and silicone fitting wing, the QuietComfort Ultra Buds family is one that has a particular style that it has stuck with for a long time.

In a recent development, pop them in your ears and you soon notice the difference. They've got even better ANC than the old model, with some of the most impressive noise canceling around. They block out everything — I took them on a long train journey, and found that all of the noise of my carriage was completely unnoticeable, even when not listening to music. It's like magic, as the orchestral sound swells and the noise disappears.

The transparency mode is very good as well, and it works well if you want to order your breakfast when you're going to work. The touch controls work well, and the charging case now contains a wireless charging coil so that you can more easily keep them fully charged.

Battery life is still not the best, though. Six hours with ANC on isn't quite up there, and four hours when you turn on 'immersive audio' is lackluster. It's not really worth turning the Immersive Audio setting on anyway.

Sources indicate that it just thins out your music as it tries to distribute it around an artificially extended soundstage, and uses up an extra two hours of battery life. The soundstage is wide enough as it is, and the sound improved over the first model for some great audio as well.

They're still the best ANC buds you can get your hands on, and the Gen 2 just cemented their place in the annals of earbuds history. That ANC is just so good.

Sources indicate that with the AirPods Pro 3, Apple was looking to unseat Bose's buds from the top of the list. Unfortunately for Apple, Bose released the refreshed Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2 just before the latest AirPods hit shelves, but the AirPods Pro 3 are still a significant step up over their predecessors.

It has been revealed that they've got sound to match the XM5, with a similarly natural sound profile and some extra juicy features that make them a whole lot more usable than the majority of the other options. They're a great jack of all trades and perfect for iPhone customers.

The ANC is, Apple tells us, "2x as good as the AirPods Pro 2". In our testing, we've found that the ANC is, indeed, much better than the ANC of the previous models. It's better at blocking out sounds across the frequency spectrum, although it still focuses on the sounds you'll hear in your day-to-day life.

That means that bus journeys are more comfortable and office stays more tolerable. The transparency mode is natural-sounding as well and gives you more battery life.

According to recent reports, there are some extra features on board the AirPods Pro 3. There's a heart rate monitor and Live Translation, although we found these to be novelty extras as opposed to 'reasons to buy.'.

According to recent reports, there are meaningful improvements in some other key areas, however. Fit is far better, and it seals very well in the ear to help the ANC. The battery life is excellent, with 2 hours more than the previous model, bringing them up to par with the Sony earbuds.

There are a couple of drawbacks. Android users won't like their less impressive features for their OS, but you were probably eyeing up the buds from Sony and Bose. There's still only one color option — white — and I've got AirPods that have died permanently gray after spending too much time in my black jeans pocket.

The AirPods Pro 3 are still an excellent pair of buds for iPhone people, however, and some of the best ANC buds around.

There are good budget buds, but there are very few as impressive as the CMF By Nothing Buds 2A. If you weren’t already aware, CMF is Nothing's most affordable product range, and the 2A sit at the bottom price rung of the brand's earbud lineup.

You might have thought that such a low price would mean low-quality ANC — but no, that’s far from the truth. The CMF Buds (sorry CMF, I’m not typing “by Nothing” every time) 2A are a budget revelation when it comes to keeping unwanted noise at bay.

We found that the sound of buses and other public transport was blocked very well by the buds, making sure that your commute is more comfortable. It’s adaptive as well, changing and shifting depending on the ambient noise levels.

Sources indicate that transparency mode was great when we wanted to order some lunch, with clear sound when we were chatting with the service staff. It’s not quite up there with the AirPods Pro 3 or the Sony WF-1000XM6, but then you could buy nearly ten pairs of these for the same price as either of those.

According to recent reports, they’re comfortable too, with loads of fitting options in the box so that you can dial them in according to your specific fitting preferences. The battery life is solid with 35 hours on tap — that’s plenty to get you through a week's worth of work and commuting. Multi-point makes sure you can connect to different devices without the need to dip into the settings menu, and it works well.

They’re obviously not perfect — some compromises have been made to keep the price down. They feel a bit cheap, and there’s no auto-pause when you take them in and out of your ears. But again, when you consider the price, the few cons are very easy to forgive.

Sound is impressive, and there are loads of extra features in the Nothing X app like a customizable EQ. We love the CMF Buds 2A, and we think you will too once you’ve got the $30 wonders in your pocket — and you want to keep the noise of your busy 7:30 AM train at bay.

Recent findings suggest that sony has been trying to take the ANC fight to Bose since the latter released its finest, and sometimes Sony has come out on top. In this case, though, it’s the runner-up — but it's so close. There are still key reasons to pick up the WF-1000XM6 instead of the QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2.

But about that ANC; it’s very good. We tested the buds in a range of different environments, from the office, a train, a busy city, and more. The noise cancellation kept out just about everything, and didn’t affect the sound of the music we were listening to.

According to recent reports, it loses out to the QuietComfort in the smoothness of the delivery. That means that changes in environments are handled slightly more roughly than Boses pair, with a little noise leaking in before the algorithm takes notice. To be clear — it’s so close. If you don’t try both, you won’t notice. Side by side though, there is an edge to the Sony that’s not present in the Bose buds.

The sound, though, is better than Bose’s buds. There’s more delicacy up top, and they’re less low-end heavy. Sony’s tuning is more pleasing to our ears across a range of different genres, making them a better bet for the sound-quality-conscious. The AirPods Pro 3 sound even better, though.

Sources indicate that they’re comfortable too, with a solid range of different tips for different ear shapes. The buds themselves a slightly strange shape, and the case is a dumb shape (it's covered with angles, so it’s less comfortable to fit in a pocket than the lovely smooth Bose and Apple options), but this is still a stylish and comfy pair of wireless earbuds.

Battery life is… fine. It’s unimproved from the previous model, the WF-1000XM5, with around 8 hours of use with ANC turned on. That’s more than the Bose buds and around the same as the AirPods Pro 3. Still, we’d like to see more battery life from flagship earbuds, considering how much you get with more budget buds.

So in the end, it all comes down to a couple of things. If you want the best noise canceling, buy the Bose earbuds. If you want something with great ANC that works with an iPhone, then get the AirPods Pro 3. If you want something that works well with everything, offers great ANC and excellent sound quality, then pick the Sony WF-1000XM6.

Industry observers note that the Noble Fokus Amadeus bring a certain class to proceedings. They're covered in a very regal red colorway, and the buds themselves have a resin finish that makes them look almost like jewelry. And I love them.

Industry observers note that they're super comfortable, especially if you use the flanged eartips. Those will also make your ANC better, and it was already really good. The highs are incredibly detailed, the mids are incredible, and the bass is impactful. They sound excellent — hence why they're on the list.

They lack some of the features of the competition, like the Spatial Audio of the AirPods and 360 reality audio you'll find on Sony buds, but they more than make up for it thanks to their incredible sound.

For audiophiles looking for their portable audio fix, the Noble Fokus Amadeus are the buds for you.

Fitness buds are a dime a dozen, with plenty of options available should you want to listen to music while you work out. The Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are the latest buds from Apple's subsidiary, and they also happen to be the best buds for fitness fanatics. They've got a useful fitting hook on each bud, and then heart rate monitors to make sure they stay in place.

Recent findings suggest that the noise canceling, as you'd hope, is excellent. I found it perfect for most different settings, be that a quiet office or a bustling train. I'm not known for my exercise, however, so I spoke to someone who is — and what they thought of the noise canceling on board.

In a recent development, they took them for months of long running sessions and other fitness work, and found they blocked noise very well. Gyms silenced, annoying traffic brought to nothing. If you want to make sure your jogs, cycling, or even your swimming is distraction-free, then the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are the buds for you.

Industry observers note that I was also very impressed with the battery life of the buds. Industry observers note that sound does trip up slightly. Industry observers note that samsung’s buds have never topped best lists, but they’ve always had a space reserved. While they might not have the same “all things for all people” vibes as the Sony WF-1000XM6, the ultra-impressive noise canceling of the Bose QuietComfort Ultra, or the Apple user features of the AirPods line, there has been little better for users of Samsung’s phones than Samsung’s buds. Industry observers note that wired earbuds are back, and there’s no bigger sign than Bose’s noise-canceling version of the format. If you’ve not experienced the likes of the upper ANC echelons, these are going to be perfectly serviceable for everyday use. They’re just a little weaker than some of the other options on this list, with some higher sounds making their way through the barrier.

Recent findings suggest that transparency works well enough, making sure that you can hear what's going on the other side of the buds without all the extra noise around you. It does affect the sound of the buds slightly, however, so you’ll pay the price in sound quality when you’re ordering your McDonald's breakfast. The price you pay for a double sausage and egg McMuffin, one supposes.

The sound quality is a highlight of the Noise Canceling Wired Earbuds. The bass is less in your face than prior models, although it’s a lovely addition to the table. Similarly, high-range and lower-register mids sound great no matter the genre you’re listening to. It's a less in-your-face audio experience than previous Bose products, which is a nice change.

Then there’s the wire, which comes with both pros and cons. You don’t have to worry about battery life, for one. The power for the ANC is pulled straight from your phone or laptops battery, so your earbuds will only die when your listening device does. That’s good. You also get lossless audio thanks to the USB-C connection, and low-latency listening should you want to play games or watch movies and TV shows on the go without the sound getting behind what’s going on on-screen.

It has been revealed that the bad thing? You’re tethered. Forget to unplug them or take them out when you stand up and you’ll send your phone flying across the floor or violently disconnect them from your laptop. You’ll need to get used to it, that’s for sure. But for under $100? It’s well worth the trade-off, if not only for effectively unlimited battery life.
