Read our full Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro Max review.

We've judged the best noise-canceling earbuds on several factors: audio performance, battery life, Bluetooth range, call quality, comfort and fit, and the effectiveness of the noise cancellation. We also weigh special features, such as included apps, and how easy they are to use.

During the testing phase, our reviewers wear each pair of earbuds for 2 hours at a time throughout the course of a week, to test comfort over time.

Recent findings suggest that ANC, meanwhile, is tested in both indoor and outdoor environments where ambient sounds are produced at high levels. This includes airplanes, city parks, convenience shops, offices, and public transportation. ANC earbuds programmed with transparency modes are also tested thoroughly to determine how well the listener can hear their surroundings.

Industry observers note that for sound quality, we listen to many different sample tracks and span as many music genres as possible, including hip-hop, rock, jazz, classical and R&B, while evaluating volume, clarity, and fullness. Find out what we listen for during our testing process and how to get the best headphone sound for you.

And now that more streaming music services are offering high-resolution audio, be sure to read our audio codec FAQ for all you need to know.

According to recent reports, finally, we’ll rate noise-canceling earbuds on our five-point system, with 1 being the worst and 5 the best. If a pair is particularly excellent, with a robust range of qualities, we may award it an Editor's Choice badge.

It has been revealed that the first item to check off the list when shopping for the best noise-canceling earbuds is their active noise cancellation performance, which shouldn’t be confused with passive noise cancellation. What are the differences?

It has been revealed that 1. Active vs. passive noise cancellation: ANC uses advanced circuitry and microphones to pick up noise signals and create inverse waves that cancel out these sonic disruptions, whereas PNC physically isolates high-pitched sounds through the headphone design and materials. Most headphones advertised with noise cancellation are categorized under ANC.

2. Battery life: Noise-canceling earbuds have a reputation for sucking up lots of power, so you’ll want a pair that holds a charge long enough to get you through a long business flight or weekly commutes. Noise-canceling wireless earbuds are usually rated for 4.5 to 8 hours, but with included charging cases the total possible playback time might be much more competitive.

Sources indicate that think about how long and how often you’d want to wear your earbuds for on lengthy trips. A longer “per charge” battery life is better, but if you only want some entertainment on short commutes then it not quite so notable, as you’ll probably be storing the buds in their case more regularly.

According to recent reports, 3. Sound quality: ANC technology can compress sound and reduce dynamics, which may affect audio performance when turned on. In some cases, you’ll notice a background hiss when listening to music. However, the best noise-canceling earbuds limit these disruptions to deliver full, crisp sound.

It has been revealed that 4. Design: The look, build and feel of a pair of in-ear 'buds is massively notable when selecting the best noise-canceling earbuds, so consider how they look and feel and whether the style is right for you. In our best noise-canceling headphones round up we mention that over-ear headphones tend to give the best noise cancellation, but some of the more recent wireless in-ear models are proving to be just as effective.

Sources indicate that 5. Pricing considerations: Obviously, price is a significant consideration when looking for the best noise-canceling earbuds. Although there are always exceptions, big-name brands will typically command a bit extra, but generally speaking, the less you spend on a pair of headphones the greater the chance that sound and features will be compromised. Going for a budget option isn't always the best choice, as any money you save on your purchase won't do you much good if you're constantly needing to recharge your audio gear, or the sound quality is poor.

ANC explained: Active noise cancellation (ANC) models employ built-in mics to pick up ambient sounds around the wearer. An identical but inverted audio signal of the noise is played back to the listener through the headphones.

Listeners aren't aware of this happening of course, as the inverted (or out of phase) signal effectively 'cancels out' the noise of the surroundings for the headphone wearer. The process removes the external sounds, which results in a significant reduction in the level of background noise at the very least.

Given that it uses both more computational power and a bunch of microphones in order to work, ANC has an effect on your battery life. This often chops a couple of hours off, so they won't last quite as long. If you want to keep the battery going for longer then you'll want to keep the noise canceling turned off.

In most cases, noise-canceling earbuds are very effective at reducing ambient sounds. There are limits, though, and some designs are less effective at silencing certain types of sounds than others.

The process is fast but it can’t physically occur in real time, so active noise cancellation (ANC) works best with consistent low-frequency sounds as opposed to higher-pitched, inconsistent sounds like human speech.

Vehicle engines and droning air conditioners are easy to cancel out, but the shorter wavelength of high-frequency sounds, like a sudden blast from a car horn, makes it tougher for the ANC’s anti-noise waves to perfectly mask these bursts.

Even so, all sounds will be at least a little quieter when you’re wearing noise-canceling headphones, and many sounds can be completely silenced even on low-cost pairs or earbuds.

Why Black Friday Is the Perfect Time to Start a Gym Membership

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most people are probably waiting until Jan.
  • Industry observers note that the week of Black Friday can deliver you a good discount on a gym membership, an empty gym, and a built-in two-month runway to turn a generic resolution into a real habit.
  • It has been revealed that this week is as good a time to save of a gym membership as a fresh air fryer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most people are probably waiting until Jan. 1 to start getting in shape, whether they want to start fresh or absolve themselves of their perceived holiday indulgences. Every year, people start the new year by joining a gym crowded with others newly resolved to get in shape, paying full price for the privilege of waiting in a long line to use the squat rack. This year, try something different: Start your gym membership during Black Friday.

Industry observers note that the week of Black Friday can deliver you a good discount on a gym membership, an empty gym, and a built-in two-month runway to turn a generic resolution into a real habit. While you're comparing deals on fresh tech, headphones, or smart home devices, here’s why you should also take a few minutes to scout out the gyms near you.

It has been revealed that this week is as good a time to save of a gym membership as a fresh air fryer. Here are just a few examples of the offers out there right now:.

Orangetheory and F45 have various free-month and prize-entry promotions for new Black Friday sign-ups, and similar studios for Pilates, yoga, and strength training have discounted multi-month and annual packages.

Independent gyms, university rec centers, and local studios often run their own versions, from a free month tacked onto a longer commitment to waived joining fees.

According to recent reports, deals vary a lot by location, so call or stop by the clubs near you and ask what's available. Then remember to always read the fine print before you sign:.

Look at the price after the promotion ends, not just the first month's rate.

Ask about fees, including joining, annual, and access fees.

Try before you buy. Many gyms offer a free trial pass. It might make sense to first visit at the time of day you'd actually go.

In a recent development, be honest about distance. The best gym is the one you'll actually walk into, so pick one that's close to home or work.

Industry observers note that gyms also run sales around New Year's, so a good Black Friday offer isn't the only deal you'll see. Even still, the savings aren't the only reason to go now.

December is reliably the quietest stretch of the gym year: People are busy with holiday travel and work deadlines, and many tell themselves they'll "start fresh in January." That means open benches, free treadmills, and staff who have time to show you how a machine works.

Recent findings suggest that that's a gift for any gym-goer, but especially if you're latest. Learning your way around a gym is much less intimidating when it's empty. You can figure out the equipment, make your mistakes in peace, and build a routine before the January crowds arrive. Plus, this time of year is a perfect window to set and achieve a winnable goal.

From Black Friday to Newly introduced Year's Day is about five weeks. By the time the January rush hits its peak and settles into its usual patterns, you could be eight weeks into a new routine. And as my colleague Beth Skwarecki explains, you really can get a lot stronger in 24 workouts. Beginners tend to see the fastest gains of their lifting lives in the first couple of months.

Prefer running? I know I do, and luckily, a couch-to-5K strategy works the same way. Most programs run about nine weeks and build you up gradually from short run-walk intervals. Start the week after Black Friday and you'll be running for a solid stretch by early January, and you'll be well on your way to 30 minutes at a stretch by the end of the month. By the time your Upcoming Year's resolution friends are just starting, you'll already be a few runs in.

In a recent development, this is also the season when many workplaces and health aims wrap up their open enrollment periods, which makes it a smart time to check what wellness perks you already have. Before you pay full price for anything, look into:.

Workplace wellness programs, which sometimes offer gym reimbursements, discounted memberships or fitness stipends.

Health insurance perks, since some looks include gym memberships or discounts.

HSA and FSA rules, where general gym memberships usually don't qualify, but some medically recommended programs may. Also check any year-end deadlines for money you'd otherwise lose.

Corporate and employer discounts, which many large gyms offer on top of regular promotions.

Stack a workplace benefit on top of a holiday sale, and your cost per workout can drop considerably—well before New Year's resolution time arrives.

#109085. Tech Report: Cento fine foods has been sued for “tomato fraud”

Tech Report: Cento fine foods has been sued for “tomato fraud”

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3813 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slate

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that so you’ve decided to make homemade pasta sauce.
  • Recent findings suggest that first stop: browsing the supermarket for the best canned tomatoes for your future marinara.
  • You’ve heard that phrase before somewhere—the Food Network?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that so you’ve decided to make homemade pasta sauce. Good for you, chef!

Recent findings suggest that first stop: browsing the supermarket for the best canned tomatoes for your future marinara. Now you’re deciding between Hunt’s, Mutti, Bianco DiNapoli, Cento, DeLallo, and those nondescript cans of tomatoes from The Bear filled with wads of cash. You’re considering brands, price points, and whether to buy your tomatoes whole-peeled, crushed, or diced, or hmm … maybe that jar of Rao’s would be easier? Then, just when you’re about to give up, two little words on a label stand out: San Marzano.

You’ve heard that phrase before somewhere—the Food Network? Ina Garten? That’s supposed to be primo stuff, right? Probably can’t go wrong with tomatoes that are actually from Italy. They’re a few dollars more expensive than the domestic options, but you spring for a can or two anyway. Surely getting the real thing will be worth the hassle and cost once that first forkful of al dente pasta and perfect sauce hits your lips.

In a recent development, san Marzano tomatoes are indeed considered the good shit. They’re cherished for their low water content (think naturally saucy, thick tomatoes), their sweetness, and their deeply savory flavor—all qualities that can make or break a marinara. And they are certainly Italian: San Marzano tomatoes come from the Agro Sarnese-Nocerino region of southwest Italy, home to the fertile land surrounding Mount Vesuvius, the volcano that once destroyed Pompeii but whose ashy eruptions, settling over time into a nutrient-dense soil, now more helpfully produce the prized fruits in question.

Authentic San Marzano tomatoes are regulated—at least in Europe—by the Consorzio di Tutela del Pomodoro San Marzano dell’Agro Sarnese-Nocerino DOP, which I will be shortening to “the Consortium” so we don’t all go insane. And the Consortium is serious about its job. According to its regulations, true San Marzanos must have an elongated shape that usually measures between 6 and 8 centimeters and demonstrate that classic balance of sweet and tart flavor. The thin skin peels off easily, enclosing dense, fleshy pulp with very few seeds. They must possess something called an axis ratio of no less than 2.2 + 0.2, or contain limited presence of “placental voids,” which means the seed cavities are filled with gelatinous tomato gel and pulp rather than empty space. In short, they’re the jackpot if you are looking to make an unforgettably robust sauce or lip-smacking soup, and the Consortium exists solely to be this marvelous tomato’s protector.

Recent findings suggest that there’s a reason these elite tomatoes are so tightly controlled. They can be grown only in a tiny region of the world—fewer than 1,000 acres of eligible volcano-adjacent land are right now cultivated—so they’re in very short supply. Or at least they ought to be. A skeptic might ask how the hell such prestigious produce ended up available in bulk at your local Ralphs or Whole Foods. Are all the brands touting the name actually San Marzanos? Is that even possible?

It has been revealed that according to a recent lawsuit, the answer is … not necessarily. In fact, some of them are almost certainly fake. It’s been called “tomato fraud,” and it’s a real problem in the U.S. Fraud may seem like a dramatic word to apply to a tin of tomatoes, but given the considerably higher cost of cans labeled “San Marzano” (recently between $6 and $8, compared to between $3 and $5 for a normie 28-oz. can in my local market), where there are fakes, honest consumers are being ripped off by companies looking to profit from a legendary culinary reputation that isn’t theirs to claim. And tomato snobs aren’t taking it lying down.

It has been revealed that over the past 10 years or so, lawsuits accusing brands of tomato deceit have become quite ordinary. Take, for example, the highly entertaining San Merican lawsuit. The short version is that a manufacturer named Simpson Brands in Pennsylvania labeled its cans “SMT,” and in exquisitely sneaky fine print, the text by each letter spelled “San Merican Tomatoes,” instead of “San Marzano.” Though the plaintiff ultimately dropped the suit (and Simpson denied the allegations), I think its claim—that a reasonable person could easily confuse these impostors with the genuine article—is certainly fair. (Oh, and by the way, those San Merican tomatoes are trash. Not even close to San Marzanos. San Mericans are watery and sour Roma tomatoes, not the thick, sweet San Marzano variety. How to tell? Squeeze one of the San Mericans in your hand, and it’ll burst everywhere as if you just unloaded a shotgun on a jar of Prego.).

While you do see “San Marzano–style” tomatoes sold quite frequently, as this verbiage merely refers to the botanical genus of the tomato and passes muster in the U.S. (somewhat like the general cheese term “Parmesan” vs. Parmigiano-Reggiano, which has its own official minders), straight-up labeling something San Marzano that isn’t would seem to run afoul of false-advertising prohibitions and leave violators open to litigation. (The Consortium might not like it, but it has no power this side of the Atlantic.) So you’d think companies would, you know, avoid doing that. Just stand behind the tomatoes you’ve got.

Sources indicate that but there’s one well-known brand that may have thrown caution to the wind. It’s one you’ve definitely seen on your grocery store shelves, one that’s available in both old-school Italian delis and high-end grocers alike. And it may have succeeded in duping everybody—at least according to the folks suing it for $25 million in damages. In the eyes of these litigants, the dignity of the Rolls-Royce of tomatoes—and the integrity of America’s food system—is on the line. The questions they raise about product quality, corporate transparency, and the weight of authenticity could shape what we stir into our pots and spoon into our mouths for years to come.

It has been revealed that in early May, a lawsuit was filed against Cento Fine Foods Inc., claiming that the firm’s iconic yellow cans of tomatoes sold as San Marzano can’t possibly be the real deal: Cento Fine Foods, a Upcoming Jersey–based company, versus Natalie Gianne of Los Angeles and Mike Aldrich of Whittier, California. The crux of the suit is that authentic San Marzano tomatoes possess physical characteristics that render them superior to other tomatoes, and so what’s in Cento’s cans is simply not that. The filing alleges that Cento’s tomatoes “lack the taste, consistency, and other physical characteristics associated by consumers with certified San Marzano Tomatoes.” Thus, they were deemed “unsatisfactory” to the plaintiffs, who never would have paid a premium for them had they known the truth. And naturally (this is America), they’re seeking millions of dollars in flavor harm.

In a statement to Slate, Cento said that it “refutes all of the inaccurate and wrongful claims” in the complaint, calling it “entirely without merit.” The manufacturer added that it is seeking a “prompt dismissal” of the suit. The Weston Firm, the lawyers representing the plaintiffs, did not respond to requests for an interview.

If this all sounds kind of hard to prove in court, I’d say you’re right—taste is subjective. But that’s where the Consortium is supposed to come in. In 1996, the European Union granted the Consortium the exclusive right to certify and approve San Marzano tomatoes, empowering it to stamp authentic cans with a DOP/PDO label (meaning Product of Designated Origin). When you see that seal, you are being promised that what’s inside is verified. And Italians live to protect their products. They protect their cheese with DOP labeling, and they even have their own pizza rules: See the AVPN (the True Neapolitan Pizza Association), which aims to tell you what a Neapolitan pizza is and, more importantly, what it isn’t. In this case, the AVPN, which approves true Neapolitan pizzerias through a rigorous application process, even goes so far as to dispatch secret agents to later spy on pizzerias. If they aren’t meeting the organization’s high standards, they’re delisted. The Consortium, meanwhile, also inspects, approves, and occasionally delists tomato purveyors with the same critical eye.

So Italy has made rules for its San Marzano tomatoes, and Europe enforces them, at least in theory. Over there, you can’t just 3D-print some tomatoes, put them in a can, and call them San Marzanos. If you did, you would be the subject of police or judicial raids (which, as we’ll see, Cento may know something about). Here in the U.S., however, those rules don’t apply: There is technically no legal protection of that term as such, which is why alleging false advertising or consumer fraud—not getting the product you think you’re paying for—would be a shopper’s only avenue for justice against perceived trickery. This Gianne-Aldrich lawsuit argues that the Consortium is the only entity that can certify and approve San Marzano tomatoes grown in Italy, and here’s the thing: Cento is not acknowledged as a legitimate producer by the Consortium. Meanwhile, the company doesn’t even hedge and label its tomatoes San Marzano–style. Cento seems to be saying, “Bitch, these are San Marzanos,” and then raising its fist in the hope you’ll flinch.

According to recent reports, how does Cento do it? Well, according to the lawsuit, it goes around the Consortium completely and has a third party certify its tomatoes (a process that, for its part, the organization defends in detail on a dedicated webpage—one that clarifies, in very small print, that its certification partner is not affiliated with any consortium). That’s why its cans read “Certified” but don’t feature the official DOP seal. Feels shady, no? Why did Cento sidestep the Consortium to begin with? If its product is authentic, why not just obtain that official seal to avoid such headaches?

The answer is where things get real juicy: Cento used to be a participant in the Consortium, but over a decade ago it was reportedly ejected from the organization for what certainly looks like—you guessed it—tomato fraud.

In 2010, according to the current lawsuit, “police in Salerno obtained a criminal search warrant and raided Cento’s Italian operations.” What they found were 144,000 cans of intentionally mislabeled tomatoes. Manager Giuseppe Napoletano was busted for distributing tomatoes bearing counterfeit DOP labeling. Napoletano was also found to have “forged the signatures of tomato farmers” and to have “repeatedly committed fraud in order to obtain false certifications.” In 2019, an Italian court found Napoletano and his father, an accomplice, guilty of criminal fraud, for which they received fines and were given 26-month suspended sentences. What’s not clear is whether Napoletano did these things at Cento’s direction or acted alone. In my research, I found no evidence that Cento has ever commented on the incident directly, though it has characterized its exit from the Consortium as voluntary. Moreover, when I emailed the company to get a comment on Napoletano and the fraud, I heard nothing back.

But San Marzano tomatoes are a moneymaker, a prestige purchase for foodies everywhere. Cento clearly couldn’t lose its cash cow. After exiting the Consortium, though, claiming that it was hawking authentic San Marzanos would be tricky. The solution, according to the lawsuit: Get its tomatoes blessed by a “third-party certifier” called “Agri-Cert.”.

In a recent development, “The hell is Agri-Cert?” I asked while reading the official court documents. Soon, I found myself obsessing over the organization’s comings and goings, its staff, its operations. Near as I can tell, the organization (also known, and findable online, as Bioagricert, which I’ll use going forward) seems to have one gig, and that gig is certification. It stamps products as organic, vegan, regenerative, and the like. But it also certifies traceability, meaning it traces an ingredient to its source. The lawsuit against Cento claims that Bioagricert doesn’t “possess the capabilities” to ensure that Cento’s products meet the same specifications as those overseen by the Consortium. Nonetheless, the plaintiffs have submitted photographic evidence of labels and website copy from Cento that call out Bioagricert (styled “Agri-Cert”) as its third-party certifier by name.

Sources indicate that so what’s the deal with this mysterious outfit? After weeks of attempting to make contact, I finally got a response from the organization that may have sliced this can wide open. Technical manager Salvatore Sergi explained its relationship to Cento via email, which … well, read it for yourself.

“We do not certify Cento products,” Sergi wrote. “Rather, we certify an Italian organization exclusively for the ISO 22005 standard (supply chain traceability). The peeled tomatoes are sold in the United States by our certified company inside unlabeled cans. These products are accompanied by a certificate that makes no reference to San Marzano tomatoes, as they are protected by PDO status throughout Europe. Cento applies its own label to the anonymous cans directly in the U.S. (where there is no protection for PDOs), due to the lack of a mutual recognition agreement with the EU.”.

He summed it up in one sentence: “In conclusion, our certification is valid only in Italy for our company.”.

To recap, Bioagricert certifies the traceability of the tomatoes—where they come from, yes (which might be key in, say, an outbreak of foodborne illness), and in this case, Cento’s assertion that they are grown in the correct region. Bioagricert does not, as Cento arguably insinuates with its labeling, certify that these are true San Marzanos with the same detailed Consortium characteristics (though Cento does claim to adhere to some of them, such as length, independently). And it doesn’t certify that because it literally can’t. That’s the Consortium’s territory. What’s more, Sergi indicates, the cans arrive in the U.S. unlabeled. It is only in America that Cento apparently applies the “San Marzano” and “Certified” labels. (Cento’s site claims the tech giant has a “production facility” in “Campania’s San Marzano growing region.”).

According to recent reports, in any case, you, chef, should not have to be concerned with tracing the international supply chain. You are in the pasta aisle. You pick up one of those yellow cans. There’s no DOP/PDO label; instead, there’s a green ribbon with the word Certified struck across it. Confusing? Yes, but as with a lot of products sold in America—from honey to olive oil—our government says you, the consumer, are required to read the fine print. Again, this shouldn’t be an glitch: An entire organization exists to protect San Marzano tomatoes. Alas, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration doesn’t play by Europe’s rules, and vice versa—according to an investigation by the Italian news station RAI 3, Cento’s “San Marzano” tomatoes wouldn’t actually be able to be sold in Italy. It would be illegal to label them as such.

Sources indicate that back across the Atlantic, will Cento finally pay the piper? Andrich et al. v. Cento Fine Foods Inc. is still undecided, but I should note that a much more scathing lawsuit from 2019 was thrown out. That one claims that the “Find My Field” tracker on the back of each Cento can—which you can use, CIA-style, to locate the exact coordinates your tomato came from—takes you to the same four fields over and over again. “It is implausible that [the] defendant can sell more San Marzano tomatoes than all other companies in the U.S., combined, and do so by cultivating only four fields,” the suit read.

Implausible indeed, but a New York judge dismissed the case, citing that your average person wouldn’t expect San Marzanos to be labeled with the Consortium’s DOP seal: “Here, while there may be ‘some few consumers’ who expect that a San Marzano tomato must be certified by the Consortium, the Court concludes, drawing upon common sense and common experience, that the vast majority of reasonable consumers expect no such thing. It is much more likely that consumers expect tomatoes grown in a region of Italy.”.

Perhaps. But one rule I live by is that you should never assume that your audience is dumb. While your average person might be unaware of tomato fraud, people who care about food care about what they’re buying. And with each passing lawsuit and news story, it’s getting harder to buy that we’re getting true San Marzanos at all. In fact, the whole thing has me second-guessing my entire tomato reality.

Sources indicate that at this point, you might want me to answer: Which brands of San Marzanos are trustworthy? We could consult the Consortium, of course, but I’m starting to think that may not be the right question. That, instead, might be: At the end of the day, when you’re just trying to get dinner on the table in your own kitchen, does any of this alleged tomato fraud even matter? Who, if anybody, is hurt by it?

Well, for starters, I would say that the farmers in the Agro Sarnese-Nocerino are deeply affected. These are generations of San Marzano growers. Many of the farmers are handpicking the tomatoes without using machines. A San Marzano tomato isn’t only its genus; its identity is fully wrapped up in the process of growing and harvesting—the region, the soil, and the methods of the farming itself. So long as San Marzano imitators exist, then the work of these hardworking farmers will be undervalued. In addition, Italian brands like Gustarosso, Casa Marrazzo, and Flora, which all adhere to the Consortium’s rules, are undercut by fakes.

Sources indicate that but personally speaking, I find myself with a moral dilemma. Because, friends, in my opinion as a food writer and avid pasta-maker, I have to confess: Cento’s “San Marzano” tomatoes are actually excellent. They are, near as I can tell, the best available tomato at the most supermarket chains. I’ve praised Cento in similar terms in the past, before undertaking this head-spinning journey into the gelatinous placental void, but even knowing what I know now, the fact remains that Cento’s tomatoes are sweet, savory, deep, and saucy. They are perfect for a red sauce. And I’m not the only one who thinks so.

“Before I opened SheWolf, I tried over 50 cans of tomatoes,” claims Anthony Lombardo, chef and owner of acclaimed Italian restaurants Medusa and Shewolf in Detroit, “and Cento was the best.” That’s high praise not only because of Lombardo’s expert taste as a professional, but also because he has gone further than most in trying to capture that San Marzano essence here at home.

According to recent reports, “It’s not like cheese or wine or salami,” he indicates, “where the DOP or DOC has real validity because it has to be this grape, has to come from this species of animal, or be this exact milk to be called this cheese.” Lombardo’s point is that tomato seeds are easily grown in other climates. Hell, I just saw a sign for “San Marzano tomatoes” at the Santa Monica farmers market, and a woman walking past exclaimed to her partner, “Oooh! San Marzanos!”.

According to recent reports, lombardo may or may not have recently smuggled some San Marzano seeds back directly from Italy, which he may or may not grow at an urban farm in Core City, a few miles outside Detroit’s downtown area. He demonstrates me a picture of green plum tomatoes growing on a vine, which he has dubbed “Detroit San Marzanos.” “Literally the opposite of a volcano,” he notes of their terroir. I ask Lombardo, who has ventured to Italy numerous times, if his Detroit varietal tastes the same as true, Consortium-certified San Marzanos. “They do not,” he says. So will the tomato police come for Lombardo? Probably not, because of the 80-some tomato plants he has, which are thriving, none of the fruit will be labeled and served as San Marzano tomatoes. Smart man.

“I get why [the Consortium] are pissed. This is, like, their thing,” he admits. “But what do I call this tomato that is clearly the shape and size of a San Marzano?” It’s a great question. San Marzano–style? Sans Marzanos? Marzano di Detroit? Is the distinction even important when we live in a country where so many things are mislabeled?

Sources indicate that italians argue that it’s not just their genealogy that makes their prize fruits San Marzanos, but their terroir. Their land. It’s that sweet, sweet volcanic soil, and the lore that comes with it, that everyone is so horny for. But more than that, it’s the culture of Italy that is worthy of being protected. Their very identity is wrapped up in these tomatoes, and when nefarious operations find a loophole, well, it can feel as if they’re crushing that identity in the palms of their hands like an Italian nonna making red sauce.

In a recent development, I get all that. And yet … I’ll say it again: Cento is currently selling the best can of tomatoes—widely available, anyway—here in the U.S. While arguably not up to Italy’s standards, the tomatoes are still wonderful in flavor and texture. These are fleshy, elongated fruits dunked in a viscous sauce, with a deeply savory flavor one would expect of, gulp, San Marzanos. I pick one up, squeeze it softly and let the plum tomato break apart gently in my palm. It doesn’t burst with water. It just sort of dissolves. I eat a piece right from the can. It’s thick and sweet, and perhaps that judge was right: It’s so good that I can’t find it in me to care about where exactly it comes from. And ultimately, I feel a little ashamed about that.

Sources indicate that but should I? I understand the value of cultural heritage, and in my heart of hearts, I wish we lived in a world that cared about authenticity, or even just the concept of a shared reality. But I don’t have to tell you that’s not where we are. Do I hope Gianne and Aldrich win their lawsuit? If their claims of fraud are true, then, yes, justice should be served. I’m tired, nay, exhausted, of living in a country where we’re constantly questioning what’s real. Where the people in charge have us second-guessing our good sense. I will concede that if this all comes down to a simple taste test, then Cento’s tomatoes are quite good. But I’d be fully willing to trade that quality for some goddamn clarity. For some honesty. For something tangible and trustworthy that I can pick up and hold. Without that, it’s hard to enjoy how good the food may taste.

So, I will simply ask Cento one thing: If the produce in the yellow cans are not bona fide San Marzanos, just drop the ruse, man. Drop the wishy-washy “Certified” label, and let the tomatoes do the talking—they can definitely speak for themselves! That way, we can all shut up, stop clogging up the courts, and get back to the thing we want to do most: making some damn pasta.

In a recent development, temperature is an key signal to our circadian rhythms, as we naturally cool at night. Increased temperatures — whether through environment our physiological causes — can disrupt your sleep quality.

In a recent development, that's why active climate control is the main focus of the Eight Sleep Pod 6. Its raison d'être, if you will. The integrated water tubes are at work throughout the night to subtly adjust the temperature of the surface.

According to recent reports, I'm not a regular hot sleeper but hormonal shifts mean a few times a month I can expect a stuffy morning. Since using the Eight Sleep, I haven't woken up sweaty once. I have on occasion felt my body temperature rise — but the Eight Sleep responds with a flood of cool.

Before bed, I've been enjoying the opposite. The Eight Sleep gently warms in the minutes leading up to my bedtime, so I climb into a cozy bed And I don't have to warm the entire house to do so — I've often found turning the thermostat up before bed results in overheating around 3 a.m.

Industry observers note that the Eight Sleep provides a gentle ebb and flow. It warms around 10 p.m., cools as I fall asleep, maintains that cooler feel until the early hours, then gradually warms again so I wake up cozy. And if at any point my body temperature or the room diverts course, the Eight Sleep can adjust to bring me back to the baseline.

Industry observers note that the Eight Sleep has a temperature range of 55°F/12°C to 110°F/43°C. This isn't the placebo effect; the Eight Sleep really is changing the feel of your mattress.

You control the Eight Sleep via the Autopilot app, which is where you set alarms, adjust temperature and view your sleep tracking data.

Overall, I've been impressed with the sleep tracking and how it's displayed in the app. Autopilot shines when it comes to data comparison, showing how your sleep is changing night by night. It's a good way to identify patterns and spot issues before they become major problems.

In a recent development, however, you don't have to use the app to control the Eight Sleep (ish). While the tracking and set up is all done via app, you can adjust the temperature in the night using a panel on the side of the cover. At 3 a.m. when your room is a touch chiller than you want but you don't want to cope with the glare of your smartphone, this is a real benefit.

Industry observers note that ✅ You regularly overheat at night: I've felt first-hand how the Eight Sleep reacts quickly to excess warmth with a sudden burst of cool. If night sweats are destroying your sleep quality, it could be a smart investment.

#109080. Industry News: The Artificial Monkey Mind

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1388 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Co ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: The Artificial Monkey Mind

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1388 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that I’ve been practising meditation for decades, but I’m barely a beginner.
  • It is not possible to stop this kind of thinking.
  • Maybe someday I’ll manage whole seconds of this ideal state.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that I’ve been practising meditation for decades, but I’m barely a beginner. What I find most challenging is what the Buddhists call the monkey mind. Instead of being aware of the moment, my brain is elsewhere. It’s dwelling on the past or worrying about the future, rather than paying attention to what’s happening right now.

It is not possible to stop this kind of thinking. That’s just what brains do. The goal is to let my thoughts go and not get caught up in them. I practise regularly to learn how to remain detached from that chaotic stream, to just observe it and not follow or react. I want to be able to make conscious choices about where I spend my attention.

Maybe someday I’ll manage whole seconds of this ideal state.

Sources indicate that it occurred to me recently that we are now dealing with a kind of artificial monkey mind in large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT or Claude. They mimic our own thinking so well that we anthropomorphise them. They appeal to our monkey minds in a way no previous technology has. I’m talking daily with people who seem to be verging on an unhealthy connection to these things, using them like a therapist or a GP, for example. They’re getting caught up in the chatbot’s responses, just as we get caught up in our thoughts.

It has been revealed that but despite the technical twist, this isn’t a fresh problem. People have been trying to tame the mental chatter and instinct-driven behaviour for thousands of years. From ancient Hindu and Buddhist traditions, through early Christian and Islamic contemplation, to modern mindfulness, humans have been struggling to rise above the clattering cacophony since at least the beginning of civilisation.

LLMs are a uniquely powerful distraction, but I wonder if these practices could teach us to interact with them in a healthier way.

The part of the mind that “thinks” is the “doing” part of our brain. It’s a what-if engine or analyser, taking often fragmentary and incomplete evidence from our senses and building a theory of reality in real time. By necessity, the mind fills in the gaps in its data. It confabulates. It’s not hallucinating, exactly – we’re not hearing voices – but we are unknowingly making up facts to fit our current picture of the world.

The brain also has basic assumptions, many of which are wrong. My impostor syndrome, which I’ve written about before, is one example of that kind of distortion. There’s also depression or other forms of mental illness.

Industry observers note that but the tendency to misread reality is more basic than that and affects everyone. Our instincts come into play. For example, getting along with others in the tribe, troop or herd has kept us alive for millions of years, so it’s a powerful urge.

With our eagerness to find patterns and our subconscious instincts, it’s no wonder that we have a hard time staying in the moment.

With chatbots, it’s even worse. We dealing with two monkey minds that play off each other. We assume we understand what the LLM – that statistically generated, stochastic parrot – is on about (pattern matching), agree with it and just become its yes man. Our instinct to gel, to go with the flow, is also triggered. An LLM doesn’t just sound like another person. It sounds like one who’s eager to agree with us. Flattery goes a long way!

In a recent development, the counterpart to the thinking mind’s “doing” mode is our “being” mode. This is our awareness, our consciousness, or what some call the soul. It’s where we experience reality. Meditation in all its forms aims to help us get to a state where we are fully aware of the present moment (the only moment we have, really) and where we are fully free to experience it, just as it is, with as few distortions as possible.

Detaching from our monkey mind, with its bad assumptions and distortions, is part of developing wisdom. At its most basic, wisdom is a sceptical attitude toward your own thinking. The wise one has learnt that they are often wrong, that first impressions are often misleading, that the best-laid intends go awry. The wise aren’t attached to their own attitudes or theories. They readily adjust when facts don’t fit any longer.

Recent findings suggest that the daily practice of meditation is like exercising the mental muscles we need to walk this path. We gently bring our attention back, without judging ourselves for drifting. In mindfulness, for example, we connect with reality in a simple, physical way: focusing our attention on the sensation of breathing. The key skill is to notice when we’ve been carried away from the present moment. It’s this, in particular, that I think will help us most with LLMs.

So, when our minds or an LLM deliver a verdict with confidence, we should say “That’s nice” or “Good boy” and treat it as another hypothesis to test. Instead, we fail to notice that we’re being carried away by this stream. We stop paying attention.

Sources indicate that of course, as my decades of flailing with meditation have taught me, it’s a lot easier said than done. As a general rule, we’re pretty helpless in the face of the egotistical monkey mind. It’s our mind, after all, and we’re pretty attached to it. We give it the benefit of the doubt, completely unconsciously. And LLMs do a pretty good job now, and are getting better, at ingratiating themselves with us.

Industry observers note that when using an LLM, it’s really tricky to remain engaged – to bring ourselves, fully and attentively, to what we’re doing. It’s very easy to get lulled into the flow with an LLM – just like it’s easy to daydream.

I mostly use LLMs for programming, so what works for me might not work for people who use them for other kinds of work. The aim is to stay present and grounded. One trick I use is to make my LLMs speak “caveman” – simple, no unnecessary words, no fluff. Just the facts. I’m less likely to treat them like people or to get stupefied by a wall of words.

Another method is to use the LLM to proposal, but do the work myself. I took a similar approach with Stack Overflow. I’d search for an answer, but I wouldn’t paste it into my code. I’d type it out, line by line. Just doing that engages your attention surprisingly well. I find myself making small changes, more fitting to my style, taste and the actual specifics of the problem at hand, even if I’m just copying someone else’s work or following another’s plan.

Finally, and most importantly, I limit my use of these things. Do I need to use an LLM for this? If I’m so lost in the code that I can’t work out where to make a small change, something’s wrong. I’m no longer in charge.

In a recent development, when I first started using LLMs for coding at work – mostly for auto-completion – they were quite clunky and stupid. But modern models are getting good. They almost feel miraculous. On code I’m especially familiar with, I can use LLMs to offload a lot of drudgery. When I know the architecture and the trade-offs that have been made, I can set the guardrails correctly and ask for specific things to be done – and the work gets done, like magic, much faster than I could do it by hand.

It has been revealed that but over time, if I continuously use LLMs to do everything, the code becomes less and less familiar. I start losing touch.

Now that I’m retiring, I’m wondering if it makes sense to use LLMs at all. At work, when I need to upgrade the runtimes of a dozen AWS Lambda functions by a particular deadline, I can justify using LLMs to churn through those kinds of tedious tasks much faster and more efficiently. But at home, I don’t have those kinds of time pressures. I’m doing the work because I’m having fun learning something fresh. I learn best by doing, by trial and error.

What am I using LLMs for, exactly?

12 Things to Do on Christmas If You Don’t Celebrate

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1019 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a way, the Christmas season is more fun if you don’t celebrate it.
  • You can’t go wrong with some moo shu pork and a trip to the multiplex.
  • If Chinese food isn’t your thing, look at restaurants serving any non-European cuisine—Greek places, Japanese places, and Mediterranean places are usually open, as are plenty of Italian restaurants and steakhouses.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a way, the Christmas season is more fun if you don’t celebrate it. You get to enjoy all the brightly colored lights your neighbors put up, but you don’t have to put up your own. You don’t have to do any duty-shopping. There's no pressure. But Christmas Day itself leaves you in a mostly shuttered world that feels like there’s nothing going on. Fortunately, there are options to make Dec. 25 a fun day off, regardless of your observances.

You can’t go wrong with some moo shu pork and a trip to the multiplex. Chinese restaurants and movie theaters traditionally stay open on Christmas Day for those who don't celebrate, and they’re often filled with fellow Christmas refugees. Check Google for the hours of your local Chinese restaurant and give them a call to make a reservation. If you’re more adventurous and you’re in a city large enough to have a Chinatown (or a whatever-town), just head straight there on Christmas and see what happens—that’s how the best days usually start.

If Chinese food isn’t your thing, look at restaurants serving any non-European cuisine—Greek places, Japanese places, and Mediterranean places are usually open, as are plenty of Italian restaurants and steakhouses. Just make sure you check first. Lots of chain restaurants are open on Christmas Day too, including Applebee's, McDonald’s, Benihana, and more. You can even get Christmas breakfast at your local IHOP. But not every location of every outlet follows the same hours.

As for movies, most chain multiplex theaters are open on Dec. 25, and theaters are usually pretty full. The movies attract both people who don't celebrate Christmas and people who do, but want to get away from their families for a couple hours, so make sure and reserve a seat beforehand. Consider hitting up an out-of-the-way spot or that theater with the table service and cushy recliners to make it feel like more of an occasion.

Most people going to the movies on Christmas Day aren’t there for Christmas movies, so interesting “secular” movies are often slated for release on the 25th. This year's Christmas is unusually packed with interesting new movies, including family flick Jumani: Open World, a Robert Eggers horror movie called Werwulf, and the crowd pleasing football story Mr. Irrelevant, so you have serious options.

Industry observers note that chinese restaurants and movie theaters aren’t the only establishments open on Christmas. Here are some other options:.

Go skiing or snowboarding: Most mountains are open on Christmas, and the lift lines are blissfully empty. There's no better way of celebrating a winter-based holiday than on a wide-open mountain.

Visit a skating rink: Speaking of winter sports, ice skating rinks are generally open on Christmas too.

Sources indicate that pretend to be a tourist: Tourist attractions are often open on Christmas, especially in larger cities. This includes places like Madame Tussaud’s and Ripley’s Believe It or Not, as well as ziplines and Segway tours—so do that touristy thing you’ve never done before.

Get a room: If you’ve got some spare cash and have nothing better to do, get a room at a hotel. Hotels don’t usually close on Christmas, and they typically offer plenty of amenities, so take advantage of the pool at the Holiday Inn or the spa at the Four Seasons, depending on your lifestyle.

Hiking and biking: Hiking trails and parks are open on Christmas if you want to get outdoors. If you’re into biking, hit the trails or hit the streets: Traffic is minimal on Christmas, so it’s a great time to put in some serious roadwork.

According to recent reports, volunteer: Not having anything to do on Christmas isn’t the biggest life problem, especially compared to people who have nowhere to go and nothing to eat. So use Christmas to help people and actually deliver on that whole “good will towards men” thing. Check your local Craigslist for volunteering opportunities.

Sources indicate that use Christmas as a catch-up day: This is strictly for type-A people, but if everyone is out of town and no one is going to call you, why not spend the day catching up on neglected chores or personal projects? You can spend at least part of your day knocking a few things off your to-do list and the rest of the time relaxing. That way you’ll get a break and still feel accomplished.

Just sleep all day: Type-B personalities like me see a day free of obligations and other people as a golden opportunity to do as little as is humanly possible, a day to fully commit to sloth.

Spend time with friends and family at home: Not celebrating Christmas doesn’t mean you can’t spend the day with family and/or friends. Get together with your loved ones, play games, watch a movie, cook together, talk, or whatever else you all enjoy. You don’t have to go out to have fun, so don’t rule out staying in with people you care about.

Shopping: This is at the bottom of the list because it’s iffy. Drug stores and convenience stores like 711 are usually open on the 25th. Grocery chains like Kroger’s and Trader Joe’s usually aren’t. Your local shopping mall or retail district might be open, but probably won't be, so check ahead.

Because so many places are closed on Christmas Day, you should plan ahead (unless you like spontaneity and are OK with the possibility of disappointment) by:.

Making a list of the places you want to go.

Calling nearby locations to confirm they’ll be open, as not every chain follows corporate holiday hour recommendations.

Making reservations at any restaurant(s) you strategy to visit.

Putting together a basic timeline of the day, accounting for travel time, so you don’t lose any reservations, miss a movie, or arrive after the store closes.

The most key advice here is to do something intentional on Christmas, even if it's sleeping in, so the day doesn't feel depressing or empty. So hit the slopes, suck down some dim sum, or keep your couch from floating away, but be sure you make Christmas your own.

I’ve been testing the Coros Vertix 4 for 5 days — here’s what I like and dislike about the Garmin Fenix rival so far

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1496 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Coros has debuted the Vertix 4 as its new flagship smartwatch, and it’s a major upgrade over the Coros Vertix 2S with an AMOLED display, a more attractive design that has a built-in flashlight, and satellite maps.
  • I’ve been testing the Vertix 4 for five days, which isn’t nearly enough time to get through its extensive battery life, but I have been able to get some first impressions of the watch by doing four runs with it, comparing it directly to the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro.
  • You’ll find my early likes and dislikes for the Coros Vertix 4 below, along with its price and specs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Coros has debuted the Vertix 4 as its new flagship smartwatch, and it’s a major upgrade over the Coros Vertix 2S with an AMOLED display, a more attractive design that has a built-in flashlight, and satellite maps.

I’ve been testing the Vertix 4 for five days, which isn’t nearly enough time to get through its extensive battery life, but I have been able to get some first impressions of the watch by doing four runs with it, comparing it directly to the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro.

You’ll find my early likes and dislikes for the Coros Vertix 4 below, along with its price and specs. For those wondering why Coros went from 2S to 4, skipping a Vertix 3, it’s to bring the Vertix 4 into line with its other watches: the Coros Apex 4 and Coros Pace 4 Pro.

In a recent development, the Coros Vertix 4 launched on 24 November 2026 and will be available to order from 27 November. It costs $799 in the U.S. and £669 in the U.K., a $100/£70 price rise on the Vertix 2S.

In a recent development, it does come in significantly cheaper than the latest Garmin Fenix 9 line-up, though, which starts at $999. However, there are some rivals that come in cheaper than the Vertix 4, with the Suunto Vertical 2 titanium model, costing $699/£639, and older Garmin Fenix models appearing in sales — the Garmin Fenix 8 is $749 at Amazon right now, for example.

The Vertix has previously had a memory-in-pixel (MIP) display, and while that does have some advantages, most notably longer battery life, I much prefer the AMOLED display on the Vertix 4.

It’s a very substantial, bright screen and easier to read than the MIP display on the Vertix 2S in all conditions I find, even in bright sunlight.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The new satellite maps also look great on the display, and the battery life on the Vertix 4 is still very good.

While it would have been great for Coros to make the Vertix 4 available with both MIP and AMOLED options, as Garmin does with the Fenix, it’s perhaps not practical in production terms, and I do think AMOLED is the better option here, with the Apex 4 offering a MIP alternative in the Coros line-up.

Adventure watches are, by design, big and bold devices to strap to your wrist, but the Vertix 2S was a little too huge, and the Coros Vertix 4 is a much more enjoyable watch to wear all day.

It’s thinner and lighter than its predecessor while having a larger display, and doesn’t feel too bulky even on my slim wrist.

In the past, I think Coros watches could be accused of prioritizing substance over style, which is no bad thing, but it’s better to have both, and both of the brand’s 2026 launches — the Pace 4 Pro and now Vertix 4 — have been more attractive than past options.

Ever since Garmin added a built-in flashlight to the Fenix 7X, it’s been a feature that people have wanted in their smartwatch, and the Vertix 4 is the first Coros watch to get it.

Coros has swerved from the usual flashlight setup used by other brands, though, sticking its light on the side of the Vertix 4, between the digital dial and back button, as opposed to on the top as Garmin, Suunto and Amazfit do.

This has its advantages — the flashlight naturally focuses the way your arm is pointing, and you can switch the orientation of the buttons on the watch if you wear it on your right wrist.

I’m still on the fence about whether I prefer this or having the flashlight on top of the watch, but ultimately it’s a substantial addition to the Vertix line in general, and a very handy feature to have.

Another interesting new feature on the Vertix 4 is satellite maps, which you can download to the watch and use instead of the standard maps. This is a feature I’m testing in beta, with it expected to launch in early 2027.

The satellite maps look great on the AMOLED display, and at times, it's a bit clearer to see what’s around you using them, especially in the forest.

It was pretty quick and easy to get my local area onto the watch through the Coros app, though the satellite map files are larger than the standard, so you will want to be choosy with the areas you download to the watch.

While the standard maps on the watch work fine, having the satellite option is useful at times, and it differentiates the Vertix 4 from other brands since these maps are free.

The Vertix 2S offers incredible battery life — it lasted me 22 days on a charge and even outperformed the Garmin Enduro 2 on this front.

Given the switch to an AMOLED display, the fear would be that the Vertix 4 fell short on this front in comparison, but the listed stats are still very impressive for the watch.

Coros suggests it will last up to 30 days in watch mode, or 10 days with the screen always on, and it offers 48 hours of multi-band GPS tracking with the screen always on.

So far, the Vertix is on track to beat those estimates for me, although aided by the fact that I haven't used it for sleep tracking so far.

With the screen always on and running every day using the most accurate multi-band mode, it’s on track to last over 10 days.

All the Coros watches launched over the past couple of years have impressed me with their GPS accuracy, and that’s the case with the Vertix 4 so far as well.

It has been revealed that I’ve been running with it and the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro, with both set to their most accurate mode, and checking the GPS tracks afterwards. The Vertix 4 tracks have been spot on and in line with the Fenix 9 Pro on pace and distance stats throughout the runs too.

Unlike GPS accuracy, the heart rate accuracy of the Vertix 4 has been a bit iffy in my early testing when comparing the readings to a chest strap.

In the Vertix 4’s defence, I’ve been testing it in cold weather, when optical sensors on watches do tend to be less accurate, but I’ve still been a little underwhelmed by the results.

According to recent reports, on my easy runs, it’s mostly been pretty close to a chest strap, but on a hard progression run, the Vertix 4’s readings were too high throughout. Based on my early tests, you’d definitely be wise to pair a chest strap to the Vertix 4, at least in cold conditions.

The Vertix 4 is noticeably slimmer and lighter than past versions, but it’s still quite a substantial watch, and Coros does not offer any size options, something that Garmin does with the Fenix 9.

There are the Apex 4 and Pace 4 Pro as smaller alternatives in the Coros line-up, but if you want the flagship model, you have to accept that it only comes in one size, and it’s a biggie.

It doesn’t take long when testing a Coros watch to realize that they really make sports watches, not smartwatches.

The Vertix 4 can store music, but only files you drag and drop onto the watch; it doesn’t pair with streaming services. It also doesn’t offer NFC payments, and you can’t customize the watch face as much as on rivals.

Personally, I don’t miss these smart features much, but they are a selling point not only true smartwatches like the Apple Watch Ultra 4, but also Garmin watches, which combine great sports tracking with useful smarts.
